#6276. The 8 Best Home Generators Are a Big Investment. These Deliver Reliable Power During an Outage.

Our editor-tested and researched portable and whole-home options keep appliances and other essentials running during an emergency—no matter what.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Stronger and more frequent severe weather events are making a compelling argument for investing in a home generator. A large portable generator or a permanently installed standby generator can keep your entire home powered and operational for several days, or at least keep a few critical appliances such as a refrigerator running until the power comes back on. The cost of emergency power is never a small investment, though it is an increasingly important one.

The term “home generator” can be confusing. It’s an unofficial category that includes larger portable generators capable of powering several appliances or a few critical circuits using a transfer switch (not all portable generators are built for this task). It also includes permanently installed standby generators that can automatically switch to whole-home backup power when the lights go out. Choosing the right size generator primarily comes down to how much power you think you’ll need in an emergency.

There are many reliable home generators that deliver a great deal of power. Some offer you the choice of running on multiple different fuels, while other models use an inverter that can give you quieter and “cleaner” operation. There is a nice range of prices available, too, so you can easily find a generator below that fits your needs as well as your budget.

For the generators on this list that we tested, we considered the difficulty of unboxing, assembling, and starting each generator for the first time, because few things are as frustrating as buying a tool that turns out to be unnecessarily complicated from the get-go.

Once set up, the generators we reviewed were subjected to different load conditions, including things such as power tools, home appliances, and even recharging large power stations. We assessed the features that distinguish these generators from each other, including safety features, app connectivity, and portability, among other things.

A few picks on our list have not been tested, but we included them here after considerable research, taking into account the brand’s reputation, our knowledge of its product lines, various outside reviews, and our own experience testing similar models from those same brands.

The DuroMax XP11000iH is a powerful midsize dual-fuel inverter generator, capable of keeping most homes up and running for an extended period of time. Inverter generators are a step above traditional generators because they convert alternating current (AC) to direct current (DC) and then back again to AC. This process creates cleaner, more efficient power and enables the generator to run more quietly and fuel efficiently.

Having two fuel options—gas and propane—provides a big boost of convenience by allowing you to use whatever’s handy. No gasoline? You can use the same tank of propane you use for your gas grill. It’s also parallel-capable, so you can daisy-chain it with another generator if you need extra power.

The generator is enclosed in a large, sturdy plastic casing, which makes it durable and provides a fair amount of sound dampening. Of the many gas generators I’ve tested, it may be the quietest model that’s capable of backing up a whole home, especially when it’s running on propane, which trims it down by another few decibels. At 61 decibels on a 20 percent load, it’s about as loud as a dishwasher. Most comparably sized generators go up to around 80 decibels—about the same volume as a police siren.

In addition to a full suite of essential modern safety features such as a carbon monoxide shutoff and low-oil shutoff, it goes the extra mile with lots of little touches, like remote start. The integrated battery tender keeps it ready to start, no matter how long it’s been sitting, which can be a lifesaver, too. When you do run out to check it, an onboard display shows you key stats such as hours run, current load, and voltage output.

The only downside I could find was its weight. At upward of 200 pounds, it isn’t easy to carry. It does have wheels and sturdy handles, though, so it isn’t hard to wheel around on flat, paved ground—if you can push a loaded wheelbarrow, you can push this. Not that you’ll need to move it much; it’s a very sturdy generator, and it comes assembled with the wheels and handles attached (not all generators come with those pre-attached). —Reviewed by Nick Hilden

Technically, there are cheaper generators out there, but the Generac GP9500E offers an outstanding blend of capability, quality, and durability at a very reasonable price. As such, this is where I’d steer you if you’re trying to shave down your spend.

Its 9,500-watt running capacity is slightly higher than the DuroMax’s, and it’s capable of powering all but the largest of homes. It can get a little noisy under a heavy load, but that’s common with units this size. It let out a relatively moderate purr when it was just powering the lights and a few appliances, but it became more of a roar when the heat kicked on.

With three fuel options—gas, propane, and natural gas—you get about as much versatility as you could possibly expect from a generator. A relatively large 7.5-gallon gas tank delivers a long runtime between fill-ups. And, while I was initially skeptical as to the necessity of the third fuel option, having natural gas support showed its value when a storm knocked out the power, and I didn’t have gas or propane on hand. All I needed to do was plug it into the natural gas line, and suddenly my house was the only one on the block with lights on.

Beyond that, though, it’s a fairly basic model. It has essential safety features such as low-oil and CO shutdown, but lacks elements such as a fancy digital display, remote start, or app. I don’t necessarily think that’s a problem: It can be helpful to get a piece of machinery that doesn’t go overboard with features. Its control panel is about as straightforward as can be, and it’s a cinch to get up and running.

Like my top pick, the GP9500E is exceedingly heavy. It’s also quite sturdy, though, which feels like a fair trade. The outlet covers aren’t as flimsy and breakable as with many other models of a similar price point. It isn’t completely immobile: It has wheels and handles that make it easy to cart around short distances. Realistically, though, weight is almost always going to be an issue with any generator capable of backing up your house.

Ultimately, its selling point is the price. It’s hard to find a quality tri-fuel generator for around $1,100, and the GP9500E performs well if you don’t mind losing out on some bells and whistles.

Whether you’re connecting devices individually, powering an RV, or running home backup power during a storm, this generator from Westinghouse (model WGen9500DF) covers all the bases. In addition to being dual-fuel (gas or propane), it includes both 30- and 50-amp outputs capable of powering 120- and 240-volt circuits. That means you could connect this generator to a transfer switch installed in your home using either option. And with 9,500 running watts of power, it’s enough for several critical circuits in your home, including the ones that run on 240 volts, such as a heating/ventilation/air-conditioning system, electric dryer, or well pump.

Several other features caught our attention, including a push-button electric start and stop (no need to mess with a pull cable), plus a remote start key fob. There’s an automatic low-oil shutoff, and the display provides the voltage output, frequency, and lifetime hours (this can run up to 12 hours on a 6.6-gallon tank of gasoline). The only drawback is the 74-decibel noise level. While that’s typical of generators of this type, if you're planning on using this to power an RV or camper, it may be too loud for some parks, as many limit generator noise to under 70 decibels.

While it does not offer as much power as some of the choices on our list, Champion’s 4,750-watt generator has enough capacity to run three or four critical 120-volt circuits in your home during an outage. It will also power small to medium campers and RVs via a dedicated 30-amp, 120-volt RV receptacle. Listed at around $600, this generator gives you a lot for the price you pay.

This generator uses a 224-cc engine with a 4.7-gallon fuel tank, enabling it to run for up to 14 hours (up to 10 hours using propane). A gauge displays a readout of the runtime hours and voltage output, and there’s an automated shutoff feature if the oil starts to run low. Since it’s dual-fuel, this generator can run off propane in addition to gasoline. For instance, if you are using it with an RV, you can run it off a camper’s propane tank without having to pack and haul a gas can. Likewise, with the included adapter hose, you can hook it up to a 20-pound propane tank.

There are a few drawbacks. Beyond the somewhat low wattage output for whole-home backup, there are no 240-volt outlets, so if you need that many volts to power circuits in your home for something such as a dryer or water heater, this model won’t be right for you. But if you just need something to keep some lights on and run a few appliances, this generator will get the job done and not cost you a ton of money up front to do it. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford

There are many reasons to opt for an inverter generator, but the two biggest ones are: cleaner, more stable power (important for powering electronics safely) and less noise. Loudness becomes a major factor with larger generators, as more power requires a more powerful engine. That’s why we were so impressed with this model (EU7000iS) from Honda. It delivers a lot of power but at notably low loudness levels.

It’s important to note that this is not a small generator. It weighs in at 263 pounds, making it one of the heaviest on our list. That said, we found it fairly comfortable to move around. The metal frame that houses the generator has a folding handle that locks into place and is capped with soft grips, while on the front of the frame there are strong 10-inch rubber wheels. This made it fairly easy to roll around, even up some gradual slopes.

It’s also quite sturdy. The outer casing is constructed of stamped metal and impact-resistant composite hard plastic, with two large, hinged maintenance doors that lock into place.

Once we fired up the generator, it was noticeably quieter than other models we’ve tested, even when outputting a 60 percent load. Using an app-based sound meter, we were reading around 70 decibels from 15 feet away, which is lower than you would see with a non-inverter generator. This is helped by an “Eco Throttle” mode that adjusts the engine speed to meet demand as different devices are added, but we found even the standard throttle mode was fairly quiet as well.

Other things we liked were an app that allows for remote operation over Bluetooth, ground fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) protection, a carbon monoxide (CO) sensor, and 240-volt output over a 30-amp connection, which will let the generator connect to a manual transfer switch for sending direct power to your home electrical box.

The two downsides are the cost (it’s very expensive at more than $4,000) and the fact that it can only be powered by gasoline; Honda doesn’t offer dual- or tri-fuel models for using propane or natural gas. But if those two considerations don’t bother you, the EU7000iS Inverter Generator is a high-quality machine that will keep you more quietly powered than some of the competition.

Full Honda EU7000iS 7000-Watt Inverter Generator Review

Battery-based backup systems are getting smarter and more powerful every year, making them an increasingly strong contender to fuel-based standby generators. This model from EcoFlow is one of the most powerful we’ve tested.

The power station combines a separate inverter unit with two 6-kilowatt-hour batteries for a total of 12-kilowatt-hour capacity. That’s enough to run power-hungry devices simultaneously—things such as heating/ventilation/air-conditioning systems, electric ovens and dryers, microwaves, and air-conditioning units. Add to this increased solar input, and you can recharge faster, too. For our tests, we connected this to a home electrical system in the home using EcoFlow’s Smart Home Panel 3, which acts as the automatic transfer switch.

During testing, our reviewer experienced two power outages, one for a few seconds and one for several minutes. This power station features an Emergency Power Supply (EPS) mode, which facilitates a 20-millisecond switch to backup power—without this set, it normally switches in about five seconds. During the longer outage, the switch from grid to backup power, and then back again, was seamless. It was fast enough that the lights never flickered and the internet never dropped.

Several advanced smart features stand out. The smartphone app enables you to view power usage, down to the circuit, preset what circuits get backup power during outages, manually turn circuits on and off, and schedule automated tasks such as charging and discharging. You’ll also receive notifications when the grid goes down and the backup power takes over. If you live in an area where electricity is cheaper during low-peak hours, it can also prioritize recharging from grid power by choosing those times of day.

Meanwhile, this system is highly expandable. You can add up to eight more batteries for a total of 10, and an inlet box that comes with the smart panel has three ports. You could plug a Delta Pro Ultra X, bolstered by extra batteries, into each port to increase the total energy storage up to a whopping 184.3 kilowatt-hours of capacity and 36 kilowatts of continuous output.

One of the biggest things our reviewer appreciates about the Delta Pro Ultra X and Smart Home Panel 3 is the peace of mind it gives. If the grid goes down, they know that their home systems will continue to run. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford

When AC power isn’t available, the greenest way to recharge a power station is with solar panels. However, the panel’s maximum power output often exceeds the maximum solar input, so they just can’t recharge fast enough. In these cases, whole-home, battery-based backup systems need the help of a fuel-based generator to recharge, so you’re not left high and dry if the power’s still out. That’s where the EcoFlow Smart Generator 4000 comes in.

This dual-fuel (gas or propane) generator connects to select EcoFlow power stations via a DC charging and communication cable, including the Delta Pro, Delta Pro 3, Delta 3, Delta 3 Plus, and Delta 2 Max. (Note: If your preferred brand is Anker, it also makes a fuel generator that’s compatible with some of its power stations, the 5500 Tri-Fuel Inverter Generator, which we also tested and reviewed.) This DC connection allows autonomous operation, so when a station’s battery hits critically low levels, the generator automatically starts to recharge it.

You can also recharge non-DC-compatible power stations by simply plugging them into the AC output, though it’s a slower recharge. If it’s an EcoFlow station, you can still automate startup, too, by pairing over Bluetooth. But you won’t be able to do this with other brands of power stations.

Our test editor Bradley Ford noted that EcoFlow’s app is one of the best features of this generator. Connecting over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, he used it to monitor fuel consumption and output, as well as set automated functions. He also tested how it can set the charging speed, monitor power output, and schedule times to start and stop the generator. He especially liked that the app provides a lot of useful information as well, such as generator fuel usage and estimated runtime.

Of course, it can work as a standalone generator, too, though there are some limitations. Ford notes that there are only two outlets: a 120-volt, 20-amp outlet and a 120-volt, 30-amp outlet. The latter outlet can connect to a manual transfer switch installed in your home, but it won’t be able to power any 240-volt circuits, and the total output of 3,200 watts is only enough to power a few circuits. However, he thinks it would work well for RV use, and because it’s an inverter generator, it’s better at safely powering sensitive electronics like TVs and computers. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford

Full EcoFlow Dual-Fuel Smart Generator 4000 Review

Pulsar is a relatively new brand in the generator business and doesn’t have a long track record. We first spotted it on Amazon and didn’t seriously consider its generators for testing. That was, up until our test editor needed a generator (with specific features and on a budget) after a generator failed at his solar-powered off-grid cabin. Happily, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel Inverter Generator showed up quickly and didn’t disappoint.

The generator was easy to assemble and prep, taking only 15 minutes. After adding oil, it was connected to a propane cylinder and was up and running on the first cycle of the starter. Our first task was to charge a solar battery bank during a wintertime period when there was not enough available sunlight, and it worked perfectly.

We have logged more than 20 hours of use so far, running it primarily on propane connected to a 100-pound cylinder (enough fuel to last a couple of months). This Pulsar puts out very clean power, with a claimed total harmonic distortion (THD) of less than 3 percent, which met the requirements of the solar inverter-charger I was using. Using the inverter to monitor the current frequency, we found that it was indeed very stable with minimal variance, between 59.97 and 60.09 Hz. All things considered, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel is a good value for the specs, capacity, and features. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford

True whole-home backup requires a professionally installed standby generator like Generac’s 22-kilowatt home standby generator. It’s designed to power a house that’s roughly 2,500 square feet. If you need to run specialized medical devices, work from home, or have kids who are learning from home, this model is a sound investment.

Another benefit of this bundle is that it includes a transfer switch, which is required if you’re planning to install this type of generator. It supports 200-amp electrical service, providing the backup circuits needed to power high-voltage appliances such as refrigerators and well pumps, along with air conditioning and heating systems. Plus, there’s built-in WiFi for checking the status of your generator and receiving maintenance alerts when you’re not at home.

You could just drive over to your local hardware store and buy a large portable generator to use as a home backup, but we wouldn’t recommend it. You want to make sure you’re getting a generator that can back up your home and power all the appliances, lights, and electronics inside. (Plus some extra watts in case you need them down the line.)

In addition, there are often state and local laws or homeowners association rules and restrictions around using them in residential neighborhoods. Choosing poorly or setting up your backup generator incorrectly could damage the generator or short out your house power at best, or lead to fire, electrocution, or carbon monoxide poisoning at worst.

Picking the best generator for your home starts with a little math. Ideally, you want to calculate how much energy you need to keep your house running, and buy a generator that can handle everything you want to power in an emergency, with room to spare.

The two key specs to pay attention to are the running wattage and starting wattage (e.g., 9,500 running watts / 12,500 starting watts). Running wattage is effectively your generator’s capacity: It tells you how much power a generator can produce steadily without any possibility of an overload. Starting wattage is the generator’s max output, or how much power it can produce for short, peak bursts when appliances first switch on.

When you are making your list, note what items are 120-volt and which ones are 240-volt appliances. It’s not hard to identify them. Refrigerators, small appliances, and most electronics run on 120-volt power and plug into standard outlets. Anything that requires 240 volts—electric dryers, well pumps, and HVAC systems—is either hardwired into your electrical system or has a dedicated 240-volt outlet. If you need to power the latter, the installation of a transfer switch and a generator that outputs at least 30 amps/240 volts may be required.

If you’re just looking to keep the fridge, lights, and a few modest appliances going through a short blackout, you can usually get away with a generator that supplies 3,000 to 5,000 watts. If you want to run the heat, hot water, and several appliances at once, plan on using at least 6,000 to 8,000 watts. If you think you’re going to be adding large appliances such as laundry machines and dishwashers, expect to need 10,000 watts or more.

A piece of advice we have: Once you figure out how much you need, opt for buying a generator that outputs around 20 percent more than that. It’s not uncommon to realize you need more than you thought you would.

It’s also important to consider that, while generators are certainly a hefty investment, they usually stand the test of time. Consumer-grade portable generators can run anywhere from 1,000 to 3,000 hours, sometimes more. If you run one for 100 hours per year, it should last for 10 to 30 years.

There are four basic types of generators, each with advantages and disadvantages.

The most traditional of the generator category, these run on carbon-based fuels like gasoline, propane, and natural gas. Some allow you to switch between them. Dual-fuel models add the option of either propane or natural gas, while tri-fuel versions offer all three fuel options. These generators can be small, offering as little as 1,000 watts of power output, or run very large, as much as 20,000 watts or more.

Different fuels offer different power capabilities. For example, a tri-fuel generator may offer 9,500 running watts and 12,500 starting watts with gasoline, but only 8,500/11,200 with propane and 7,500/9,500 with natural gas. Regardless of the fuel you choose, this type of generator must always be operated 5 to 20 feet away from the home or any window or door, because the carbon monoxide exhaust is deadly. Even a garage with an open door is not safe.

Often this type of generator is called portable, but that's a relative term: Almost all of them weigh more than 100 pounds, and many are upwards of 200. Many are on wheels, making them relatively easy to store in a garage and wheel outside when you need them, but actually moving one will likely require at least two people.

Inverter generators look and operate the same as other portable generators, but have an added component–a power inverter– that converts the alternating current (AC) power generated by its fuel source to DC (Direct Current), then inverts it back to AC before putting it out.

Generators without an inverter generate varying degrees of distortion in the sine wave of the alternating current, which can trigger power surges and other issues in some electronics. The inverter stabilizes the power, almost like a filter, “cleaning” it for more sensitive electronics like TVs and laptops.

So why doesn’t every generator have an inverter? Inverters are expensive, so the generators are, too.

Realistically speaking, you don’t need an inverter generator to power major appliances and your house power, but if you’re running a full home backup (or if you count a TV or laptop among your essential electronics), holding out for an inverter is a smart move.

While often referred to as “solar generators” because they can be paired with solar panels, power stations are not really true generators. They're advanced battery banks that store power, which you precharge using AC power or solar panels. They can’t generate electricity in real time.

But because they can offer many of the same electrical outputs as a fuel generator, they can function similarly to a traditional generator for as long as the batteries retain a charge. Some stations are very small and meant only for off-grid adventures like camping trips, but some are large enough to run whole-home systems that can produce 14,400 watts or more with expandable batteries.

Since power stations don't run on fuel or have an engine, they can be used indoors without the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning and operate with almost no noise.

The downside is that once the power is depleted, the power station must be recharged. If the power grid is still unavailable, it can take many hours in ideal sunny conditions if all you have are solar panels. You can use a traditional generator to recharge a power station, but some may view that as defeating the purpose.

Standby generators are permanently installed generators designed to automatically take over for your house power in the event of an outage. You can set them to power your whole house, or only specific circuits, giving you precise control. Standby generators start at around 10,000 watts (10 kilowatts) but can go up to much higher. For the average home, a range of 10 to 25 kilowatts is usually enough.

They typically require professional installation, making them the most costly option. Since many large portable generators can effectively back up a house for a few hours for a lot less money, standby models are still considered a more niche option.

When you draw too much power from your generator, its performance will start to decline. At home, your lights will start to dim or flicker, and appliances may turn off momentarily. The generator itself may also start to get louder, or sound like it’s working extra hard to keep up.

If you notice these signs, start turning off and unplugging non-essential power sources immediately, or turn the generator off entirely for ten minutes or so to reduce the power load.

This is an urgent problem, so do not wait to take action: If you overwork your generator for too long, it’s only a matter of time before it starts to overheat, produce smoke, or break down. The damage from an extended overload could permanently damage the generator or, worse, start a fire.

With the right size for your home, a portable or standby generator can run as long as you keep feeding it fuel and stay within its running wattage capacity; however, you should not run them indefinitely. Manufacturers recommend you allow them to rest for 30 minutes or more after at least 24 hours of use. Check the manual of your generator for its specific recommendations.

You will get more time from each tank of gas if you draw less power, so it helps to pay extra attention to your electricity usage when you’re running the generator.

Make sure to turn your gas and/or propane generators off when it’s time to refill the tank. Failing to do so could lead to a fire.

Power stations, since they rely on electricity or solar power, can almost always be charged while in use.

Never run a fuel-based generator (gasoline, propane, natural gas) indoors. Burning fuel releases carbon monoxide (CO), which will quickly build up to deadly levels in an enclosed space.

Set your generator up outside, between 5 and 20 feet away from your home and/or any garages, sheds, or other walls. Position it as far as possible from doors, windows, and vents, with the exhaust positioned away from the house, to minimize the possibility of fumes wafting in. If you keep it outside all year round, find a naturally covered position where snow won’t naturally pile up around it.

My generator is situated near my home’s power box, which is located on a windowless side of my home. It stands about five feet from the exterior wall, with plenty of space on all sides, but close enough to sit under the roof peak overhang 20 feet above.

David is a Reviews Editor for Hearst’s Enthusiast Group, contributing to Popular Mechanics, Runner’s World, Bicycling, Best Products, and Biography. He has over 25 years of experience writing about and reviewing consumer electronics, kitchen appliances, DIY products, outdoor gear, and more. He also spent years covering the ever-changing world of online retail. To relax, he loves experimenting with new recipes, tweaking his smart home setup, and spending time outdoors on his bike or camping.

#6275. How do tumors talk to nerves? This scientist is finding out

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Sebnem Ece Eksi wants to see how nerves change as cancer progresses. She hopes those changes could offer clues for detecting tumors earlier.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Sebnem Ece Eksi did a double take. Proteins typically studied in the brain were turning up in prostate cancer cells from high-risk patients. These proteins, called neuronal adhesion molecules, play a key role in the circuitry associated with memory.

The finding, made during her Ph.D. days at the University of Illinois Chicago, raised so many questions to which Eksi is still seeking answers. Now at the Oregon Health & Science University in Portland, Eksi has made it her lab’s goal to find out how nervous systems communicate with cancer. What were once two separate fields might be connected more closely than previously thought.

“What we’re learning is that tumors are actively communicating with the nervous system,” Eksi says. “In a way, it makes sense to me that a growing tumor in our bodies, in an organ, would be immediately sensed and detected by the nervous system.”

Eksi now plans to test an AI image-based recognition algorithm to identify nerve fibers in human patients. This is exciting, she says, because these nerves aren’t normally visible in patient tumors. But through biopsies, she hopes to map out and observe how the nervous system — which impacts sleep, cognition and pain — changes as cancer progresses. The implications are significant, she says. Could experts use the nervous system to detect cancer early? Can they improve patients’ quality of life?

“This field of cancer neuroscience can change all different stages of cancer diagnosis and treatments,” Eksi says. “It’s growing so quickly, the field itself.”

#6274. Ancient hunters in Australia had more on the menu than archaeologists expected

Ancient bones from two sites in northwestern Australia suggest that a varied diet gave hunters more options as rainfall and prey availability changed.

Ancient hunters in northwestern Australia ate a wide range of animals, and their leftovers suggest they could be choosy.

A study spanning roughly 50,000 years found that dietary variety could reflect plentiful food and skilled hunting.

The research was led by Tiina Manne from the University of Queensland. Her team examined ancient animal remains from Riwi rockshelter and Boodie Cave on Barrow Island.

A widely used archaeological model predicts that hunters first concentrate on prey offering the greatest returns. They add less rewarding animals when preferred foods become harder to obtain.

The new research challenges that reading of dietary diversity. At both Australian sites, people ate many kinds of animals from early in the occupation records.

“First Nations peoples in Australia were much more sophisticated and strategic in the animals they chose to hunt,” Manne said.

“Flexibility, not fixation on a few species of prey, was the smartest way to live in an unpredictable climate.”

Riwi stands on Gooniyandi traditional lands near the Great Sandy Desert. People began using the rockshelter about 45,000 years ago.

Its deposits contain remains of wallabies, echidnas, possums, flying foxes, lizards, and snakes. Small wallabies, lizards, and snakes dominate the earliest part of the analyzed sequence.

Boodie Cave’s first occupation dates to between about 51,100 and 46,200 years ago. Barrow Island was then part of the mainland, with its surroundings changing as sea levels fell and rose.

The team identified 1,167 specimens from Riwi and 2,083 from Boodie Cave by animal group or body size. The varied diets persisted across substantial environmental changes.

Burned bones and impact marks at Riwi helped link the remains to human food preparation. Some fractures also occurred while the bones were fresh.

“In a land of unpredictable rainfall, a variety of foods signal ‘plenty’, and flexibility was the best strategy,” Manne explained.

Some of the most revealing findings were bones still joined together, known as articulated remains. Their condition suggested that people had discarded body parts with little nutritional value.

“On Barrow Island, which was then connected to the mainland, the diet included wallabies, turtles and reef fish, and articulated bones suggest only the most nutritious parts were eaten and the rest were discarded,” Manne said.

“This isn’t the behavior of people short of food – they could afford to be choosy, so a broad diet reflected choice, not scarcity.”

The paper dates these articulated remains to around 7,200–6,800 years ago, long after the earliest occupation. Around this time, rising seas were cutting Barrow Island off from the mainland.

The researchers documented 24 groups of joined bones, including fish spines and parts of turtle limbs.

They interpret these discarded portions as evidence that people could select the more rewarding parts of their catches.

An animal’s value depended on more than its size. Weather affected both its condition and the effort needed to catch it.

“When water and vegetation were plentiful, large kangaroos were spread thin across the landscape, but in arid conditions they became easier to ambush as they stayed near waterholes,” Manne said.

“Small animals like bandicoots were also a good option when it got dry, because they stayed fat by switching to eating insects.”

“Hunters who kept their options open could shift between prey as conditions changed.”

At Riwi, large kangaroo remains became prominent after about 34,000 years ago, as conditions grew drier. The authors suggest hunting them became less risky when water drew the animals into more predictable locations.

Fat mattered, too. Opened leg bones at both sites point to the extraction of marrow, while smaller insect-eating animals could retain valuable fat during drought.

Many Australian animals hide in burrows, vegetation, or rock crevices during the day. Finding them requires knowing which traces to follow.

The paper draws on First Nations ecological knowledge, including signs such as fresh tracks, disturbed soil, and scratches on bark. These can reveal prey that a hunter cannot see directly.

“A tremendous amount of ecological knowledge is passed on in oral histories, including subtle signs of not only how to find prey, but the best prey depending on the season and circumstances,” Manne said.

Where hidden animals were abundant and diverse, investigating those signs could reward hunters with many different foods. A smaller animal could be a dependable catch even when a larger one promised more meat.

The authors argue that archaeological diets need to be understood through local animal behavior, food availability, and hunting costs.

A fixed ranking of desirable prey can miss how those factors change with rainfall.

Animal remains also reveal only part of a meal. Plant foods, documented at other northern Australian sites, would have supplied important carbohydrates alongside meat and fat.

“Importantly, our work suggests archaeologists around the world should re-consider how they have interpreted diet choice and diversity,” Manne concluded.

The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the Natural Academy of Sciences.

The BepiColombo spacecraft has overcome a last-minute computer glitch to enter orbit around Mercury — the 2nd craft in history to orbit the closest planet to the sun.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Update: On Tuesday (Nov. 24) ESA Director General Josef Aschbacher announced on X that the BepiColombo team has isolated the computer glitch, and tweaked the mission accordingly. "The remaining manoeuvres have already been replanned, with no extra burns needed," Aschbacher said. The two probes are still on track to seprate on Dec. 9. (This article was updated at 11:40 a.m. ET on Nov. 24).

After eight years slingshotting around the inner solar system, the joint European-Japanese spacecraft BepiColombo has finally entered into orbit around Mercury — becoming only the second mission ever to orbit the closest planet to the sun.

Mission scientists confirmed on Saturday (Nov. 21) that the spacecraft reached Mercury's orbit and is transmitting data back to the ground team.

However, the orbital insertion didn't go entirely as planned, European Space Agency (ESA) representatives said in a statement on Monday. Due to a software glitch, the spacecraft didn't fire its thrusters for the full 37 minutes required to slow its approach to Mercury.

ESA has investigates the issue and confirmed the spacecraft's new trajectory; meanwhile, BepiColombo remains "safe," the statement noted. The spacecraft should be ready to begin a year of intensive science observations of Mercury starting a few months from now.

An illustration of BepiColombo approaching Mercury for orbital insertion.

Built jointly by ESA and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), BepiColombo is actually two separate probes, which are currently stacked one atop the other in orbit. The ESA-built orbiter, named the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), and the JAXA-built orbiter, the Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (Mio), carry separate science instruments, and they will soon diverge into separate orbital paths around the mysterious inner planet, operating as two probes gathering different streams of data.

A selfie of BepiColombo during a flyby of Mercury's north pole in 2025.

The pair of probes launched together aboard an Ariane 5 rocket in October 2018, and spent the following eight years on an interplanetary journey that took them past Earth, the moon and Venus. It even passed by Mercury itself six times. (During one of these flybys, in January 2025, Bepi snapped an incredible closeup photo of Mercury's north pole.)

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

This complicated cosmic choreography was necessary to prevent BepiColombo from picking up too much speed and overshooting Mercury's orbit, according to ESA. Mercury sits about 36 million miles (58 million kilometers) from our star, or roughly one third of the distance between Earth and the sun. That makes it very difficult for a spacecraft to reach Mercury without being captured by the sun's considerable gravitational pull and dragged off course.

Only one other spacecraft — NASA's MESSENGER probe — has succeeded in entering Mercury orbit before, circling the planet from 2011 to 2015 after its own seven-year journey through space.

BepiColombo will spend the next few months getting both probes in position to start mapping Mercury in the greatest detail ever.

MPO and Mio are expected to separate in early December, with Mio entering a highly elliptical orbit around Mercury's poles. MPO will then take a few more months to fine-tune its trajectory, reaching a lower and more circular polar orbit in March 2027, according to ESA. Its science operations are expected to begin in April.

The sibling probes will each orbit Mercury several times a day, with MPO completing an orbit every 2 hours or so. Observing the mysterious inner planet from several different vantage points, the probes will make the most comprehensive map of Mercury ever. The mission's suite of science instruments will study the planet across the electromagnetic spectrum, taking observations in X-rays, gamma-rays and ultraviolet light, as well as collecting detailed measurements of the planet's magnetic field.

With this information, scientists hope to unravel many mysteries of the least-explored planet in the solar system. The new data should enable scientists to tackle myriad long-standing questions: What is Mercury's interior made of, and where does its magnetic field come from? How was the planet formed, and to what extent is it still tectonically active today? By making precise measurements of the spacecraft's orbit and position, a radio experiment will also provide a new test of Einstein's theory of general relativity.

Stay tuned for more updates from ESA about humanity's first visit to Mercury in more than a decade.

#6272. At the Races: Regional realignment

New England is the ancestral home of moderate Republicans, from the Saltonstalls to the Bushes, whose fiscal conservatism and social moderation defined the national GOP for decades.

Last week, Yankee Republicans suffered a near-total wipeout. Maine’s Susan Collins, New England's last GOP senator, lost her seat to Democrat Troy Jackson, leaving former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, who just won a House seat, as the lone Republican headed to Congress from the region. (The picture was a bit brighter at the state level, where GOP Govs. Phil Scott of Vermont and Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire were both reelected.)

One Republican operative sees a path out of the wilderness in a post-Trump era. In an opinion piece in The Boston Globe, consultant Kristin Tate urged New England Republicans to focus on fiscal discipline and recognize that “independence from national party leadership can be a political asset, not an act of betrayal.”

After all, as the midterm election results remind us, no political realignment lasts forever.

Three decades ago, there were plenty of moderate Democrats from Southern states serving in Congress, governor’s mansions and even the White House. But in the years since Bill Clinton's exit from the political stage, Democrats have largely written off the South.

Which is partly why last week’s Democratic wins in the Carolinas, Georgia and, perhaps most notably, Mississippi were so stunning. All the elements that powered the party to victory nationally – disillusionment with Donald Trump, a rise in economic populism and hunger for change – played a role in the South as well.

But other factors were unique to a region that has seen renewed attempts to dilute Black political power with the redrawing of House districts to favor the GOP.

The Republican redistricting gambit in Southern states did not fully yield the desired results and seems to have helped galvanize Black voters and their allies, powering Democrats to unlikely victories.

It’s too soon to say whether the GOP’s reduced hold on the South represents a temporary blip or an enduring shift.

But Joe Trippi, a longtime Democratic strategist who advised candidates in Alabama and Florida this year, has a message for his party: “We need to invest in the South.”

#MSSEN: Democrat Scott Colom defeated GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction and the first in his party to win a Senate seat in the Magnolia State since 1982.

Tar Heel tidal wave: Democrats in North Carolina have picked up at least five House seats, a striking development given the steep structural disadvantages the party faced. Prior to last week, no House Republican incumbent had lost a general election in the state since Republicans won control of the redistricting process more than a decade ago. And the Democratic gains could grow: In the 5th District, former journalist Chuck Hubbard narrowly leads 11-term Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx, and in the 3rd District, former state Rep. Raymond Smith holds a razor-thin edge over Republican Rep. Greg Murphy. The Associated Press had not called either race at publication time, though Murphy has conceded.

Republicans pick campaign chairs: Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno and Georgia Rep. Brian Jack will be the chairs of Republicans’ respective campaign committees for the 2028 cycle. GOP lawmakers held their leadership elections Tuesday, as our colleagues Savannah Behrmann and John T. Bennett reported. Senate Republicans are sticking with South Dakota’s John Thune to lead them in the next Congress, while House Republicans picked former Freedom Caucus Chair Jim Jordan as their leader.

Redistricting doubts: Maryland could be getting a new congressional map after voters approved a constitutional amendment that would clear the way for new lines in 2028. Our colleague Victor Feldman has more on the result and other election-related ballot measures across the country. But it’s not clear how many other states may look to redistrict next cycle after Republican efforts over the past 18 months largely didn’t pay off in last week’s elections.

Run the table: With Rep. Darren Soto winning a sixth term in Florida, no Democratic incumbent lost reelection to a Republican this year. Soto’s win in a redrawn district also meant that Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had targeted under a new congressional map.

California contest: Rep. Ken Calvert defeated fellow Republican Rep. Young Kim in a rare member-versus-member contest for a redrawn Southern California seat that turned acrimonious. Republicans are poised to hold just four House seats in the Golden State after Democrats made good on five pickup opportunities under a new congressional map.

Cheesecake Factory caucus: The latest episode of the Political Theater podcast, hosted by Roll Call editor-in-chief Jason Dick, breaks down how candidates in both parties fared in counties where The Cheesecake Factory operates, after the popular chain restaurant became something of a side character in the closing weeks of the midterm campaign.

Back to school: Newly elected members of Congress are on Capitol Hill this week for freshman orientation, an experience Massachusetts Rep.-elect Dan Koh told our colleague Nina Heller is “like high school – but it’s fun high school.” The incoming lawmakers took their class photo Thursday morning and will get to pick their Capitol Hill offices after next week’s famed lottery, Nina writes.

Tracking the count: As of 4:30 p.m. Eastern time Thursday, House Democrats had flipped 44 seats, while Republicans had picked up three. Twelve races remain uncalled, including a pair in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. On the Senate side, Democrats have flipped eight seats, with only Alaska’s race still undecided.

Guv update: Democrats flipped at least five governorships last week and will hold a majority of governor’s mansions next year. Two gubernatorial races remain uncalled by the AP: Kansas, where Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher is narrowly ahead of Republican state Senate President Ty Masterson, and Alaska, where Democratic former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is just below the 50 percent threshold to win the election outright. In territorial elections, Republicans flipped the governor’s office in Guam while voters in the Northern Mariana Islands will pick their next governor in a Nov. 20 runoff.

#TNSEN: Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who was elected Tennessee governor last week, is poised to pick her Senate successor. According to the Nashville Banner, the short list includes Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs, a former professional wrestler, Reps. Tim Burchett and Chuck Fleischmann, and Tennessee Deputy Gov. Stuart McWhorter.

2028 on the brain: A handful of House Democrats are already considering 2028 Senate bids, according to Axios, including Kansas’ Sharice Davids, North Carolina’s Don Davis and Pennsylvania’s Chris DeLuzio.

Senator Morrison?  Minnesota Rep. Kelly Morrison is earning buzz as a potential appointee to fill the Senate seat that Democrat Amy Klobuchar is vacating to become governor, Semafor reports. House Democrats aren’t likely to be as concerned about open seats as their Republican counterparts were in recent years, given the size of the incoming Democratic majority.

AOC’s future: Progressive activists have launched a new organization to encourage New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for president in 2028. Meanwhile, Axios reports that Ocasio-Cortez has parted ways with the digital fundraising firm she’s worked with for several years and has brought on the same firm that Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders used during his two presidential campaigns.

Women lead: Shirley Emehelu is New Jersey’s new lieutenant governor after Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill picked her to succeed Dale Caldwell, who resigned in September amid sexual harassment allegations and other ethical lapses. New Jersey is now one of five states to have women in both the governor’s and lieutenant governor’s offices, along with Massachusetts, Arkansas, Iowa and Virginia. Iowa will come off the list next year after an all-male Democratic ticket swept this year’s gubernatorial race, though five other states elected women to both offices last week.

Congress will once again be filled with losers – i.e, new members who have lost previous bids for elected office. Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections returns to his biennial tradition as he runs down the latest list of “losers.”

Ducking the wave: Democrats notched big wins in unexpected places, but one state grew redder after last week’s elections. The New York Times checks in with voters in South Dakota, where the GOP won all nine statewide elections.

Here come the MBAs: Democrats with corporate connections were among the winners in last week’s elections, countering the idea that candidates with serious business credentials have struggled within the party, The Wall Street Journal reports. The field of 19 winners with M.B.A. degrees includes Costco board member Helena Buonanno Foulkes, who won the Rhode Island governor’s race, and Paige Cognetti, a Goldman Sachs alum who flipped a House seat in Pennsylvania.

How Ricketts did it: Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts’ election night success was one of the few bright spots for the GOP. Ricketts fended off a challenge from independent Dan Osborn by painting him as a Democrat, questioning his authenticity and highlighting leaked audio of his comments denigrating Trump voters, writes the Nebraska Examiner.

Was it necessary? California redrew its congressional map to favor Democrats in response to Texas taking a similar step to boost the GOP. But some are questioning whether the state needed to cast aside its independent redistricting commission to rejigger the lines, given the scale of Democrats’ wins. “What they were literally saying is, ‘Let’s undo democracy to protect democracy,’” Lincoln Project co-founder Mike Madrid told CalMatters. “There’s something very Orwellian about it.”

Song of the cycle: The New York Times reviews “Talafreako,” an unlikely viral anthem celebrating the newly elected Democratic senator from Texas.

History does rhyme: An opinion piece in The (Charleston) Post & Courier argues that the win by Democratic Sen.-elect Annie Andrews is the latest in a long line of cases in which South Carolina voters bucked the idea of party bosses picking their leaders.

The man behind the grill: The New York Times profiles Russ Hudson, the Mississippi man in Colom’s now-legendary “Pick another protein” ad.

That was the last time Democrats won 11 House seats in North Carolina.

As of Thursday afternoon, they appear on track to match that number. They’ve already won nine seats – a mark they last cleared in the 1982 midterms – and they’re narrowly ahead in two more races.

If those leads hold, Democrats' 11-member delegation would look much different than the one sworn in some 66 years ago in 1961. Tar Heel Democrats taking office in January would include four women, six Black members and one Hispanic member.

Their 11 representatives (out of 12) in the 87th Congress were all white men who consistently voted to uphold racial segregation and oppose major federal civil rights legislation.

Vote counting in Alaska is expected to conclude by Wednesday, Nov. 18, the targeted date for ranked choice tabulations in races in which no candidate took more than 50 percent of the vote. As of Thursday, Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in the Senate race, though she’s below the 50 percent threshold.

Meanwhile, Democrats are gathering in Denver beginning Thursday to celebrate their historic wins and plot their next steps.

#6271. Virtual reality can make you feel sick even when the scene around you stays still

In a five-minute VR experiment, watching a single moving ball increased nausea, eye discomfort, and disorientation as the eyes aimed and focused at different distances.

Volunteers spent five minutes in a virtual reality headset watching a speckled ball glide toward them and away against a black background. Afterward, they reported more nausea, eye discomfort, and disorientation than before.

The ball was designed to put two jobs the eyes normally do together at odds.

As it appeared to move closer, the volunteers’ eyes turned inward to follow it, but the headset kept the image in focus at a fixed distance.

A cap of 64 electrodes recorded their brain activity shifting while it happened.

The research was conducted by Mattie Johnson, a computer science doctoral student at the University of Maryland.

Amitabh Varshney, a computer science professor and dean at the university, led the study, and Sujal Bista of the University of Maryland Institute for Health Computing was a co-author.

The team worked with the Food and Drug Administration and Sony on the study.

The team is careful about what the electrode readings mean. The scene used for comparison differed from the test scene in more than one way, and the authors can’t fully rule out eye and facial muscle activity.

So the paper calls the brain changes candidate correlates, not a signature of this kind of sickness.

Look at a real object and your eyes do two things at once: they turn inward to aim at it, and their lenses adjust to bring it into focus.

The two distances agree. A headset breaks the agreement. Its screens sit at one fixed focal distance while the 3D picture asks the eyes to aim nearer or farther.

The Meta Quest 2 used here has its focal plane about 4.3 feet (1.3 meters) in front of the eyes. The team measured that with a camera and a test pattern.

Within about half a diopter of that distance the mismatch is mild. Outside it, discomfort builds.

So the team showed volunteers a black-and-white speckled ball on a black background. It glided from 11 inches (0.275 meters) out to 4.7 feet (1.425 meters) and back, one round trip every 3.9 seconds.

The ball grew as it receded and shrank as it approached, so it always looked the same size.

The researchers designed the scene to reduce the feeling that viewers themselves were moving while still making their eyes aim nearer and farther.

Forty people, 65% of them men and nearly all between 18 and 30, took part.

The researchers analyzed brain recordings from 38 people and complete questionnaires from 38 people. Each analysis excluded a different pair of participants.

Each person sat through five minutes with eyes closed, five minutes looking at a headset’s static home screen, and then five minutes of the moving ball.

Before and after the ball, they filled out a 1993 simulator sickness questionnaire, the SSQ. It scores nausea, eye-related symptoms, and disorientation.

All three scores rose, and the total score rose by what statisticians call a large effect. Men and women both reported more symptoms, though men’s disorientation scores didn’t rise by a reliable amount.

Most participants described themselves as not at all or only slightly prone to this kind of sickness.

The electrode cap sampled the scalp 250 times a second. Software stripped out blinks and muscle noise as best it could.

The team compared 50 seconds of brain activity near the end of the home-screen baseline with 50 seconds near the end of the moving-ball scene.

In clusters of activity toward the front of the head, power in the fast beta and gamma brain waves fell. In clusters toward the back, power in the slower theta waves fell.

“In the frontal lobe, we found a statistically significant decrease in high brain wave frequencies during cybersickness, and in the occipital lobe we saw a statistically significant decrease in low brain wave frequencies,” Johnson said.

“These changes in what we call EEG clusters could be useful predictors of a cybersickness experience.”

The pattern is not the one Varshney’s group found in 2022 for the motion kind of virtual reality sickness, where slower waves grew stronger over the center of the head.

The studies found different patterns, but the researchers still don’t know whether the latest pattern reflects sickness, differences between the scenes, or both.

The baseline scene and the ball differed in brightness, content, and layout. Volunteers were told where to look during the ball but not during the baseline.

Some of the drop in slow waves at the back of the head may simply be visual processing of a different picture. The front of the head is also where eye movements leak into recordings most.

The team didn’t record whether participants wore glasses or contacts, and nearly everyone was under 30.

The authors also wrote that the headset’s three fixed lens-spacing settings fit a larger share of women than men poorly. That could add to symptoms in ways the study can’t separate.

Whether the brain changes track the sickness itself, the change of scenery, or both is the question the authors leave open.

Settling it would need a baseline scene matched to the test scene, which the authors recommend. It would also need eye tracking to remove the eyes’ own electrical traces, which Johnson’s team plans to add.

The goal beyond that is a headset that detects the pattern and adjusts the scene.

“Ultimately we want to inform technology to mitigate symptoms in real time, improving user comfort and productivity over extended periods of immersion,” Johnson said.

Bista put it as a shift in who gets asked.

“The SSQ still has its uses, but now we have the tools to go from asking participants how they’re feeling to asking the brain and body what’s really going on,” he said.

The full study was published in the journal Virtual Reality.

#6270. How do scientists learn from failure? This researcher has clues

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Cornell computational social scientist Yian Yin turns the tools of science on science itself. He’s studying how AI-assisted submissions are changing what gets through peer review.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Yian Yin seeks to understand the dynamics of science itself. The computational social scientist is particularly interested in how innovations happen and how they may be accelerated.

“I want to understand what the secret sources or recipes of success are,” says Yin, of Cornell University.

He applied machine learning techniques to accepted and rejected research proposals to understand how scientists learn from failures. What he found was that scientists fail, and they fail often. Some switched gears after some rejections, but others who continued their research and incorporated feedback found success at a faster rate. Those who changed ideas or scrapped original proposals did not leverage a lot from their experience.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“A group that’s not only failing better and better,” Yin says, “is also failing faster and increasingly faster towards their eventual success.”

More recently, Yin has been investigating how generative AI is changing scientific publishing. Journals are receiving more AI-assisted submissions than ever before, which is leading the peer-review process to falter. More seemingly well-written papers that lack substance are getting through, he found. Coming up with large-scale solutions requires looking at the issue in a measurable way, Yin says.

“Considering both the technological and social side of scientific ecosystems would be something that’s really beneficial for the ongoing public debate and discussion about how we accelerate science in the age of artificial intelligence,” Yin says.

#6268. In 1950, Michigan beat Ohio State in the Snow Bowl without a first down, and the blizzard behind it dumped up to 62 inches of snow

The Snow Bowl storm, later called the Great Appalachian Storm, contributed to at least 160 deaths and is the worst Ohio Valley snowstorm NOAA has analyzed.

On the Saturday after Thanksgiving in 1950, Ohio State and Michigan played their annual game in Columbus in a blizzard. At noon, the temperature at the city’s airport, a few miles from Ohio Stadium, was 10°F, and visibility was half a mile.

Michigan won 9-3. It did so without a single first down and without completing a pass, according to the National Weather Service. The game became known as the Snow Bowl, and some call it the Blizzard Bowl.

The storm that buried the field was much bigger than one football game. Over the following days, it dropped as much as 62 inches of snow in West Virginia, sent temperatures down to 3°F in Atlanta, and pushed hurricane-force gusts into the Northeast.

It ranks as the worst Ohio Valley snowstorm analyzed by scientists at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

The game’s place in history has little to do with the quality of the football, the weather service’s office in Wilmington, Ohio, says.

It is remembered for “the weather, as the game was played in a significant blizzard unlike any that either school had played in before, or since.”

Neither team could move the ball, so they kept punting it away. Michigan punted 24 times, and its total offense for the whole game was 27 yards. Ohio State punted 21 times, and four of those punts were blocked by the Wolverines.

All of the scoring came from blocked kicks. Ohio State blocked a punt that led to a field goal. Two of Michigan’s blocks led to a safety and a touchdown.

“It speaks to the severity of the storm, the remarkable conditions, and just how debilitating extreme weather can be,” the Wilmington office wrote.

The weather service has analyzed the afternoon’s hourly observations at Port Columbus Airport. The temperature climbed only from 10°F at noon to 16°F at 4 p.m.

Sustained winds blew at 17 to 22 mph, with gusts of more than 35 mph, so wind chills stayed between -8°F and -1°F. Visibility dropped as low as a quarter of a mile in snow and blowing snow.

Two days earlier, the weather had been very different. On Thursday evening, November 23, which was Thanksgiving Day, it was 39°F in Columbus at 8 p.m.

An arctic cold front then moved through, and by midnight it was 20°F. By 7 a.m. on Friday, the temperature had fallen to 8°F.

On the day of the game, 7.5 inches of snow fell on Columbus. The weather service says that is still the city’s record for a single November day.

From Thursday night to the following Tuesday, the city got 14.9 inches. Its November 1950 total of 15.2 inches remains the snowiest November on record there.

The cold front that arrived on Thanksgiving night was the precursor to the Great Appalachian Storm of 1950.

According to the weather service office in Jackson, Kentucky, the arctic air behind it sent temperatures to all-time November lows across the Upper Midwest and the Ohio Valley.

Chicago dropped to -2°F on November 24, tying its lowest November reading, and the next day Louisville hit -1°F and Lexington -3°F, both records for the month.

On November 25, low pressure formed over the Carolinas, the Jackson office says. It moved northwest into Ohio by the middle of the next day, spreading heavy snow as it went, then spun over Lake Erie before it weakened and left for Canada on November 29 and 30.

The snow piled up from western Pennsylvania deep into West Virginia. Several places received more than 50 inches, and Coburn Creek, West Virginia, reported the largest total, 62 inches, according to NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI). Pittsburgh got about 30 inches.

The cold reached far into the South. Temperatures fell to 22°F in Pensacola, Florida, 5°F in Birmingham, Alabama, 3°F in Atlanta and 1°F in Asheville, North Carolina, NCEI says, and the record cold damaged crops in Georgia and South Carolina.

The storm drew arctic air in on one side and warm Atlantic air in on the other. While Pittsburgh was buried under snow at single-digit temperatures, Buffalo, New York, about 200 miles to the north, had temperatures in the 40s and no snow at all, the Jackson office says.

In the Northeast, the problem was wind. New York City recorded a gust of 94 mph, and Newark, New Jersey, 108 mph. Bear Mountain, just north of New York City, had a 140 mph gust, and Mount Washington in New Hampshire reached 160 mph.

The winds caused extensive tree damage and power outages, and coastal flooding that broke through dikes at LaGuardia Airport and flooded its runways.

Fierce winds are still a feature of big East Coast storms, as earth.com saw when blizzard winds battered the coast in a more recent storm.

Heavy rain on the warm side of the storm brought near-record flooding to eastern Pennsylvania. Then, in the first week of December, unusually warm weather melted the snow quickly. The Ohio River rose to 28.5 feet in Pittsburgh and 56 feet in Cincinnati, 4 feet above flood stage in both cities.

The storm contributed to at least 160 deaths, NCEI says. Insurance companies paid out more for its damage than for any earlier storm or hurricane, according to the Jackson office. They call it the costliest storm on record up to that time. NCEI describes it as one of the costliest storms on record.

NCEI rates major snowstorms with its Regional Snowfall Index, which combines how much snow fell, how large an area it covered and how many people lived there.

The 1950 storm scored 34.7 in the Ohio Valley, the highest of the 232 storms analyzed there. The second-worst, in March 1993, scored 24.6. In that region, more than 6.1 million people lived where at least 18 inches of snow fell.

In the Northeast, it ranks ninth of 230 storms, just behind the storms of February 2003, February 2010 and January 2016.

Scientists are still studying how storms like this work. NASA-backed scientists have flown research planes straight into snowstorms to learn how their heaviest bands of snow form.

The information was obtained from the National Weather Service’s pages Snow Bowl – November 25, 1950 (Wilmington, Ohio) and The Great Appalachian Storm of 1950 (Jackson, Kentucky), from NOAA NCEI’s article The Great Appalachian Storm in Historical Context, and the Michigan vs. Ohio State team game records of the University of Michigan’s Bentley Historical Library and the Ohio State University Archives.

#6267. Would we know if lab-grown brain tissue became conscious?

Scientists propose testing whether lab-grown brain tissue can learn a pattern and detect when it changes, a possible clue in the search for signs of consciousness.

Scientists can grow small clusters of human brain cells in a dish. One set of joined clusters has reacted to capsaicin, the compound found in chili peppers, but a reaction like that doesn’t show the tissue feels anything.

Two neuroscientists have now proposed a way to check what such tissue, called a brain organoid, can do. Their plan borrows tests already used on infants, sleeping people, and patients who can’t respond.

The tests ask whether an organoid can learn a pattern and notice when the pattern is broken. The proposal reports no results, and the authors wrote that it is highly unlikely today’s organoids are conscious.

Lucia Melloni of Ruhr University Bochum in Germany and Stanislas Dehaene of the Collège de France in Paris wrote the proposal. Both belong to a brain and consciousness research program at CIFAR, a Canadian research organization.

“I don’t believe that brain organoids currently possess consciousness,” Melloni said.

“But given the pace with which the technology is advancing, they may do so in future. That’s why we need to start thinking about how we can find out.”

Organoids are grown from human stem cells. The cells organize themselves into tiny tissues that copy some features of the early developing brain.

Researchers can also fuse several organoids into what they call an assembloid. The one that reacted to capsaicin joined four organoids to rebuild a basic pain pathway.

“A reaction, however, is not proof that the tissue feels anything,” Melloni said.

Other teams have wired brain cells into machines, including one hooked to a simplified version of the video game Pong. Melloni and Dehaene wrote that those setups are too complex to show what the living tissue itself worked out.

In a 2024 study they cited, a gel that responds to electricity produced similar results in place of the cells.

The central test comes from research on how people process sequences.

A person hears ba-ba-ba-ba-bu again and again. The brain reacts to the bu because it differs from the four sounds before it.

After many repeats, the person learns the whole pattern. If the sequence then comes as ba-ba-ba-ba-ba, the brain reacts again, this time because the expected bu is missing.

The second reaction is the harder one. It depends on a memory of the whole sequence, built up over many repeats.

An organoid has no ears, so researchers would use electrical pulses or light in place of sounds.

They would stimulate two or more separate groups of cells in sequence and record how the tissue’s activity changes.

The question would be whether the same sequence produces a different response depending on what came before it.

Monkeys can learn patterns like this one too. That has let researchers study the brain activity behind the reactions in animals that have no language.

In people, the first kind of reaction survives sleep and anesthesia. The second seems to require a person to be awake and paying attention.

Doctors have also tried the test on patients who can’t communicate. In those patients, 80% of the ones whose brains showed the second reaction later regained consciousness.

The test missed many others. Only 35% of the patients who recovered had shown the reaction.

Melloni and Dehaene wrote that no single test would be enough. Their confidence would rise if an organoid passed this test along with several other known signs of consciousness.

The authors wrote that a failed test is perhaps the more likely outcome. A failure would lower confidence that an organoid is conscious.

Dehaene has a financial interest in this kind of testing. He is a co-inventor on a patent for methods to monitor consciousness and an associate at a company that uses those methods in clinics.

The authors wrote that there is no evidence current organoids hold any rich picture of the outside world or of themselves. The tissues are tiny, and they are cut off from a body and from surroundings.

Organoids can be kept alive for months to years, though, and they keep changing as they age. The authors proposed running the same tests on an organoid again and again as it matures.

Human babies show the second kind of reaction at 3 months of age, and it may be present before birth, after 35 weeks of pregnancy.

Repeated testing would show when each ability appears in an organoid.

The authors also wrote that if several signs ever pointed the same way, the ethical treatment of these tissues should change with the evidence.

Melloni and other researchers have called for an international board to oversee organoid research.

The full study was published in the journal Neuron.

A recent satellite image captured a striking scene at the Shiveluch volcano, which has been erupting for nearly 30 years in Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Where is it? Shiveluch volcano, Kamchatka Peninsula, Russia [56.66230841, 161.3449064]

What's in the photo? Snow melting around a growing lava dome at the volcano's summit

Which satellite took the photo? Landsat 9

This striking satellite snap shows a heavy blanket of snow surrounding a growing lava dome at the summit of one of Russia's most active and unstable volcanoes.

The snow-covered peak, called Shiveluch (also spelled Shivelyuch or Sheveluch), is a 10,771-foot-tall (3,283 meters) stratovolcano. The name Shiveluch loosely translates to "smoking mountain" in the language of the region's Indigenous Itelmen people. It is the northernmost active peak in the Kamchatka Peninsula, a highly volcanic region in eastern Russia that's famous for its unusually powerful and dramatically beautiful eruptions.

Shiveluch stands out even among its extremely active volcanic neighbors and is one of the planet's most active volcanoes, according to NASA's Earth Observatory. It has experienced at least 15 eruptions in the past 100 years, the most recent of which has been going on since 1999, according to the Smithsonian Institution's Global Volcanism Program.

On average, the volcano spews around 530 million cubic feet (15 million cubic meters) of lava every year — enough to fill 6,000 Olympic-size swimming pools, according to a 2007 study. As a result, its appearance constantly changes when viewed from above.

"On a near-daily basis, satellites detect new signs of activity within [Shiveluch's] horseshoe-shaped caldera, including thermal anomalies, hot avalanches and debris flows," Earth Observatory representatives wrote. The volcano is also constantly spitting out "ash deposits that darken the surrounding landscape," they added.

A massive lava dome was growing from Shiveluch's summit. It likely looked something like this dome, which grew from the same place in 1993.

In this image, you might be able to see a particularly dark circle at the top of the volcano's caldera. This is a lava dome — a steep-sided landform that emerges when lava piles up on top of a volcanic vent — that has been growing rapidly in recent months, according to the Earth Observatory.

The lava within this swelling blob is "extruded slowly and piles up into lobed, sloped, or spine-like shapes akin to those that form when toothpaste is squeezed from a tube," Earth Observatory representatives wrote.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Eventually, lava domes grow so large that they give way under their own weight, often causing the caldera's walls to collapse. However, it doesn't take long for the volcano to rebuild itself after these events. (It is currently unclear if the photographed lava dome subsequently collapsed after the photo was taken.)

"Shivelyuch is an incredible volcano that has collapsed over and over again, on several scales, ranging from enormous flank collapses to more modest dome-collapse events," Janine Krippner, a volcanologist based in New Zealand, told the Earth Observatory. "It goes through cycles of collapse but then builds itself up again and again through constant volcanic activity."

Lava flows, visible as black lines snaking down the volcano's slopes and large patches of ash (at the bottom of the image) have retained so much heat that snow cannot settle on them, despite being months or even years old.

In a zoomed-out version of the satellite image (see above), black streaks are visible at various points along the volcano's flanks, including a thick dark line emanating from the summit caldera. These are lava flows from recent months or years that have retained enough heat that any snow that lands on them soon melts away, according to Live Science's sister site Space.com.

Krippner noted that when she previously visited Shiveluch for fieldwork, she could still feel heat coming from lava flows that were over 5 years old.

Further afield, you can also see larger black streaks that look as if they have been painted onto the satellite image with rough brushstrokes. These are patches of pyroclastic ash left over from a 2023 eruption that burned down large parts of a nearby forest, according to the Earth Observatory.

A 2022 astronaut photo shows a thick blanket of snow covering Yellowstone Lake, transforming the frozen body of water into a featureless white void. But below the ice lie some of Earth's hottest hydrothermal vents.

A 2025 satellite image shows a series of ghostly ice swirls sculpted on the surface of Lake Michigan by strong winds during an extreme cold snap that covered Chicago in a blanket of snow.

A 2017 astronaut photo shows an unusual checkered pattern surrounding a river, just south of the Canadian border. The unique sight is the result of a forest management initiative dating to the 1800s.
