#6264. A morning dose of blue light may help you sleep better at night

Office workers given morning blue light for 30 minutes slept about 11 minutes longer that night and brought more energy to work the next day.

Blue light has become the villain of bedtime. Phones get dimmed at night and glasses that block it sell as sleep aids.

Yet the same light, delivered for half an hour after waking, made a group of office workers sleep longer and better that night. The gain carried into the next day’s work.

The effect was modest, about 11 minutes more sleep a night and a small lift in how well people said they slept.

Participants who reported sleeping better also reported more alertness and less mental fatigue the next day. Greater alertness was linked to more engagement at work.

Kathleen Keeler, who studies management and human resources at Ohio State University’s Fisher College of Business, led the study.

Christopher Barnes of the University of Washington’s business school and Brian Gunia of Johns Hopkins University’s Carey Business School were among her co-authors.

The glasses came from a company called Ayo, which donated half the pairs used.

Barnes said the mechanism is not a morning jolt from the blue light itself. “It’s that the blue light helps them sleep better later that night, which helps them the following day,” he noted.

The body runs on a roughly 24-hour cycle that decides when a person feels sleepy and when they feel awake.

Light is the strongest signal that keeps that internal clock on time, and blue light, in particular, is what the clock responds to most.

Blue light at night pushes the clock later and holds back melatonin, the hormone that brings sleep on.

That is the part everyone has heard. The same light in the morning pulls the clock earlier, which, in principle, should make sleep come sooner and run smoother that night.

Workplace researchers had tested the night half of that idea with blue-blocking glasses and found better sleep and better work. Workplace studies had not tested the morning half.

The team invited 200 full-time employees at a large Midwestern university, all working roughly nine to five, and 182 finished the study.

Nearly three in four were women, and the typical participant was in their early forties. They had been with the university for about a decade on average.

For 10 workdays, each wore glasses that shine blue-turquoise light toward the eyes for 30 minutes right after waking, between 5 and 10 a.m. On average they started just before 7 a.m.

For one of the two weeks the blue glasses ran at full power. For the other they ran at 1%, a glow so faint that in earlier tests people couldn’t tell the two settings apart.

Which week came first was decided at random, so every person served as their own comparison.

Participants filled in a survey each morning about the night’s sleep and their energy, and another each afternoon about their work, from engagement to helping coworkers to slacking off.

The team collected 1,259 daily surveys and registered its predictions in advance.

Each participant kept the glasses and a year of the companion app afterward.

After a full-power morning, people reported sleeping about 11 minutes longer that night, and rated the night’s sleep about 3.5% higher. Neither number is large. The team then traced the effect through the next day.

Longer and better sleep predicted more alertness the next day, and better sleep predicted less of the feeling that one’s mental energy is running low.

Alertness, in turn, predicted stronger work engagement and more helping behavior. Less depletion predicted better task performance and fewer behaviors like taking an overlong break.

Each link in that chain was small, and the team said so.

“This is a pretty small, cheap, easy intervention, and we’re getting meaningful movement on work outcomes that matter,” Barnes said.

The morning blue light didn’t increase alertness that same day.

Alertness that same day was no higher, which is why the authors read the whole effect as running through sleep.

The benefit also built across the week rather than appearing in full on day one.

Two groups gained more than the rest. People who arrived with existing sleep problems saw a bigger improvement in sleep quality.

Younger employees saw a bigger gain in sleep length, with effects on engagement and helping that the older workers did not show.

The authors tied the age gap to the eye’s declining sensitivity to light with age, and called both findings exploratory.

Barnes had a cheaper suggestion. “The best thing you could do in the morning is get outside,” he said.

Every measure here was self-reported, including how well people said they performed, so the findings wait on a replication with objective records.

Everyone studied worked daytime hours at one university, and most were women. The authors said shift workers, who often miss morning light altogether, might gain more, but no one in this study worked nights.

The measure of workplace misbehavior was also short and noisy, which the authors said may have hidden a larger effect rather than created a false one.

What the glasses add on top of a sunny walk is the open question, since the study compared bright glasses with dim ones, not glasses with daylight.

The authors said the next test belongs with people whose schedules fight their body clocks.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Applied Psychology.

#6263. What helps land recover after fire? This ecologist looks to the past

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Jennifer Grenz, an ecologist and member of the Lytton First Nation, asks how changes in the way people care for the land may have left it more vulnerable to wildfire.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In an increasingly fire-prone western North America, Jennifer Grenz, an ecologist and member of the Lytton First Nation, looks at fire with a holistic eye. She considers her work with landscapes recovering from catastrophic wildfire to be “deliberately unfocused,” spanning soil microbial ecology, restoration ecology, invasion biology and historical biology.

Grenz analyzes historical ecological records, like how Indigenous people have shaped and cared for ecosystems over time, to paint a comprehensive picture. “I’m interested in how those histories leave ecological legacies and hints of the stewardship of the past,” says Grenz, who leads the Indigenous Ecology Lab at the University of British Columbia in Canada. “What changed on the land that made it more vulnerable?”

Grenz spends time with many kinds of specialists, such as archaeologists, anthropologists and Indigenous elders who provide oral histories.

Moving forward, her lab will examine ecology below ground, including soil, microbial communities and root networks. The goal is to understand the role of underground ecology in critical topics like carbon sequestration, climate change, biodiversity and sustainable management.

“My motivation is in our interior Salish Territories in the southern interior of British Columbia, where my ancestors rest and where my people are,” Grenz says. “The responsibility I feel to them and to our Tmícw, which means our lands, [is] to not take us back to the past, but to show that we have the deep knowledge to help us move forward.”

#6262. The 8 Best Solar Generators Provide Reliable Backup Power in a Pinch

These tested and researched models from Jackery, EcoFlow, Anker, and other trusted brands are the ones we stand behind and recommend.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Power stations (i.e., solar generators) have become increasingly popular because they are easy to run, cost less over time than gas generators, and offer eco-friendly, emission-free operation, especially when paired with a solar panel. Some are small and compact, ideal for off-grid adventures, while larger ones are able to back up critical home circuits during a blackout.

Unlike fuel-based generators, solar generators can’t create electricity in real time. They’re giant battery packs, not true generators, and need to be recharged using alternating current (AC) power or solar panels, the latter of which often takes many hours in ideally sunny conditions.

Despite those distinctions compared to portable generators, there’s nothing more convenient than a power station for charging or running everything you need for day-to-day life—phones and laptops, lights, and even a small appliance or two. Plus, it’s nice to have a device that doesn’t produce carbon emissions and replenishes itself freely from the sun’s rays. Whether you’re seeking a highly portable option or need one that’s heavy-duty enough for extended use, these are the best solar generators we’ve tested and researched to date.

To pick the best solar generators, we tested some of these power stations for charging capacity, ease of use, weight, and different use cases. Our picks were reviewed by Popular Mechanics editor Brad Ford, who provided input for the larger-capacity units. Other models on this list were reviewed by test editor David Dritsas or freelance writer Maggie Slepian.

Our primary concerns were portability and convenience. Ease of use was also important—was the display easy to read? Did the screen readouts make sense? Bonus points if we could tell how much power is available at a glance. In the past few years, these criteria have become easier to meet. There are now plenty of compact, affordable units that have better charging capabilities than before.

Very few power stations of this size can handle as much solar input power as the Bluetti Apex 200. With two input types—low-voltage XT60 (up to 1,000 watts) and high-voltage MC4 (up to 2,000 watts)—it can accept up to 3,000 watts of solar power. If you had the panels and ideal weather, you could fully charge this station in less than 2 hours—even faster than plugging it into the wall. That’s impressive.

It also balances nicely between being a portable station and a home backup solution. It offers 3,200 watts of continuous power (it says 3,600 on the front, but that’s only if it’s connected to an expansion battery). We were able to power a refrigerator for a full 27 hours on a single charge, and estimated the battery efficiency at 90 percent, which is very good. Meanwhile, the 2,560-watt-hour battery capacity is expandable by adding up to six additional batteries. Using Bluetti’s largest battery, the B500K, you could build a massive 33-kilowatt-hour system.

While 3,600 watts isn’t enough to power a whole home, you could power a couple of circuits through a manual transfer switch using the 120-volt 30-amp output. But keep in mind that there’s no 240-volt support, so you can’t use it to power high-voltage appliances like electric dryers.

As a portable station, the Apex 200 has a lot to offer. At 59 pounds, it’s not too hard to move around the house or in and out of a vehicle. And there are several great DC power options, including a bank of USB outlets (two are high-power USB-C) and both 10- and 30-amp, 12-volt outputs. We also love that the AC ports can individually be turned on and off using the mobile app; this helps improve overall runtime.

Since very few stations can match its max solar input capacity, we concluded that the Apex 200 is definitely a top choice for anyone who wants a power station that can recharge using the sun’s rays, but also offers the versatility of being used on the road or at home.

Full Bluetti Apex 200 Power Station Review

This model replaces the original Jackery 1000, but many of the same observations made of the first model still apply. The new version has a slightly higher capacity of 1,070 watt-hours and uses a newer lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) battery, which is a newer battery technology that offers a longer lifespan (4,000 cycles versus 500 cycles for this model) and better performance in extreme temperatures.

Expert Maggie Slepian used the previous model on a media trip where she had to keep multiple camera batteries charged during a weeklong outing. She found that while the capacity was lower than you'll find with others on this list, it actually powers items for longer than some higher-capacity models. She also charged her photographer’s camera batteries while charging the power bank on solar power (it was a very sunny winter day), which proved effective and efficient.

The newer V2 model has seven ports, including three AC outlets, two USB-C ports (one 30-watt and one 100-watt), a 12-volt car port, and one standard 18-watt USB-A outlet. It charges a typical laptop eight times or powers a small refrigerator or an electric cooler for over 15 hours.

The Jackery Explorer 1000 V2 charges with a 200-watt solar panel or a 12-volt outlet in your vehicle while you’re on the move. It has fairly standard charging times, with 11.5 hours in a car outlet, 6.5 hours for solar panels, and just 5.5 hours to fully charge in a wall outlet. This won’t be your best bet for powering larger appliances, but it’s an ideal power station for smaller items and off-grid camping.

This power station takes solar recharging seriously. The Elite 300 can accept up to 1,200 watts of input, which is a high amount for a station this size. We paired it with a 250-watt portable panel and, on a fully sunny day, got around 260 watts of input. That’s the typical efficiency of a portable panel (again, you’ll never get 100 percent). But pair it with some larger panels, and you’ll get even more.

It also boasts an impressive battery capacity of just over 3,000 watt-hours and 2,400 watts of output, which is high for a station of this size. Plus, it includes a 120-volt 30-amp port, which is handy for connecting it to a small RV or pop-up camper, allowing you to run small appliances and water pumps. It’s not enough power to run a heating or cooling system for a significant amount of time, but for lights, small appliances, and other items that need power, this station will deliver.

If there’s one downside we found, it’s that there’s no way to add an expansion battery to increase your capacity. That’s not a huge detractor, but it’s something we’ve seen in stations even smaller than this one. But at the end of the day, the Bluetti Elite 300 solar generator offers the right balance between a midsize power station that delivers a lot of power and run time, and a station that is compact and portable enough to be perfectly suited for an outdoor adventure.

Full Bluetti Elite 300 Solar Generator Review

The EcoFlow Delta Pro is a large portable power station with an output that rivals some gas portable generators. When sold in a bundle with solar panels, like the package with two 220-watt portable panels we tested, it becomes a powerful solar generator. With an output of 3,600 watts, the Delta Pro can charge multiple appliances, and the output has the ability to bump up to 4,500 watts with its built-in X-Boost technology if more power is needed.

To get an idea of the run time, we used the Delta Pro to power a full-size, 25-cubic-foot refrigerator—which it did for a remarkable 51 hours and 24 minutes. When recharged from a standard outlet, it took only two hours and 36 minutes. But it also charges with the included adapter, at electric vehicle charging stations, with a DC car adapter, or with the solar panels that come with the unit. Through the 30-amp connection, you can also connect this to a transfer switch to directly power select circuits in your home.

Like any power station with a large battery capacity, it will take a long time, perhaps nearly two days, to recharge this station using the bundled 220-watt solar panels. The good news is the Delta Pro accepts up to 1,600 watts of solar input, so it can charge faster by connecting more panels.

The heavy-duty wheels and telescoping handle on Anker’s Solix F3000 are easy to use, allow you to stand upright when pulling, and are a dream for people who regularly find themselves moving their power station around, whether it’s at a campsite or to different parts of the house during a power outage.

Along with convenience, this generator is a powerhouse with the capacity to easily run your refrigerator or a greenhouse heater, or keep your RV bright and warm.

We were impressed with Anker’s app, which allows us to check the charging status or power being generated without continually going outside to check. The app also lets you turn the power to the AC and USB ports on and off remotely, keeping tabs on how much energy is being utilized.

The Solix F3000 has 11 ports, including two car ports, an RV-specific outlet, four AC ports, three USB-C charging ports, and two USB-A. In sunny conditions and moderate temperatures, it recharges with a 400-watt solar panel in just a few hours and supports up to 2,400 watts of solar input.

One of Jackery’s most recent solar generators is also its most rugged, able to withstand the elements better than most. It achieves this with an IP65 weatherproof rating, molded rubber port covers, a shockproof enclosure, and a bottom drainage system, which is part of a titanium alloy cooling structure that helps keep water out of the enclosure.

We got a chance to see these features up close and were impressed by them all, as well as a very sturdy enclosure that, thanks to the cooling system design, eliminates any side vents that could allow water to get inside. It feels strong; you could bang this station around without worrying too much about damaging it. The only downside is that this denser construction adds a bit of weight.

As a power station, it delivers 1,800 watts of output with a battery capacity of 1,536 watt-hours. That’s enough power for a weekend camping trip or for running low-powered small appliances and some lighting during an emergency. As a solar generator, it can handle up to 800 watts of input from a portable panel. We paired it with a Jackery 200-watt panel, and it worked well. Overall, if your off-road adventures often get a little dirty, but you need some extra power, the Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Power Station is a good one to have at your side.

Full Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Power Station Review

The latest version of the Goal Zero Yeti 1500 is a well-designed power station that’s ideal for off-grid camping situations where dust, wind, and potentially wet conditions are always on the table. This 2,000-watt power station is weatherproof with an IPX4 rating and features outlet shields that cover the ports and inputs. Each section is well-lit by an LED light that’s individually turned on or off using a manual button or the mobile app (and will shut off if not used after a certain period).

There’s a healthy number of outputs on the Yeti 1500, including four 120-volt AC outlets, four (two are high-powered) USB-A ports, and four 12-volt connections. We simulated an emergency blackout and managed to run a cable modem with a WiFi router, a lamp, a TV, and a tower fan, while charging a phone and a laptop through the USB-C ports. Given the station’s output and capacity, there was enough power for over two days of use (conveniently shown on the main display), and there was plenty of room to spare for a few more devices.

To test its solar capabilities, we paired the Yeti 1500 with a Nomad 200-watt portable solar panel and connected it using the high-voltage DC input, which accepts up to 600 watts; however, it also features a low-voltage input that accepts up to 300 watts for smaller panel arrays. Because both inputs can be used simultaneously, you could theoretically pair with two arrays for up to 900 watts, which is a high amount of input for a station of this size.

Of course, no portable panel operates at 100 percent efficiency. Even on a sunny, cloudless day with no shade-causing obstructions, the input readings showed anywhere from 125 to 145 watts. After initiating a recharge with only 5 percent capacity left, it would take at least 10.5 hours in those conditions to recharge. That’s actually not bad. An average of about 70 percent efficiency for a portable panel is good.

The Anker Solix C2000 power station can deliver the full 2,400 watts of output to the bank of five AC outlets—something similar stations don’t offer. This allows you to power several things at once, like a refrigerator, toaster, router, and chargers, all at the same time.

During our tests, we were able to take full advantage of this, powering a refrigerator (by itself for up to 18 hours), along with some high-powered appliances, like a four-slot toaster and an electric kettle (though not the last two at the same time).

Another interesting ability of the C2000 is that you can fast charge it from AC power up to 1,800 watts, but that recharging rate remains consistent if you’re powering other devices at the same time (we confirmed this with a wattmeter). For example, we ran a 1,400-watt space heater while still recharging at the full 1,800-watt rate. Other power stations offer similar fast charging but will throttle the amount of power coming into the station while powering devices.

For solar recharging, we were a bit disappointed that this station can only accept 800 watts of input; other stations of this size accept more. But when solar was plugged in, it worked well. We connected it to a 200-watt Anker portable panel, and in full sun, we were getting around 125 to 145 watts of input, which is pretty good as these types of panels go. The C2000 is not IPX-rated for any type of weather resistance, however, so we would not recommend leaving this station sitting outside if the weather turns wet.

Full Anker Solix C2000 Power Station Review

Power stations use watts and watt-hours to express size and capacity. Watts (size) refer to how much power it produces. For example, if you need to run a 900-watt microwave, you’ll need a station that outputs at least that much power (ideally more, since factory specs are never exact).

Meanwhile, watt-hours (capacity) give you an idea of how long devices can be powered continuously, though how much time depends on the amount of power being drawn—watt-hours don’t dictate a set time frame. Higher-powered devices will drain the battery a lot faster than lower-powered ones.

That may seem confusing, but a simple equation gives you an approximate idea of how it works: total watt-hours (of the generator) ÷ watts (of the device) = hours the power station runs.

For example, if you had a power station with a 2,048-watt-hour capacity and wanted to run a 750-watt space heater consistently at its highest setting, it would probably run for around 2.5 hours, so long as nothing else is plugged in. But for a refrigerator, whose power draw fluctuates between 10 and 300 watts (depending on how often the compressor turns on), you might be able to run it for nearly 24 hours.

Keep in mind that manufacturer specs are taken from perfect conditions; in the real world, you’ll likely see slightly less capacity from your power station. If you’re not sure how much power the different devices in your home draw, sometimes it’s written on a label, or you can use a device like a wattmeter.

Just as a power station has specifications on output size and capacity, solar panels are rated by how many watts they produce for a device after they convert the sun’s rays into electrical current (e.g., 100 watts, 200 watts, etc.). Because real-world conditions are never perfect, it’s not uncommon for panels to only output 50 to 75 percent (or even lower) of their total potential.

Your panels must also be within the acceptable input range of the power station. For example, connecting a 400-watt solar-panel array to a power station that only accepts 110 watts of solar input can cause an overload and damage the station.

While weight and size don’t directly correlate to the technicalities of power banks, they impact the convenience of each model. Many camping and overlanding setups have limited space, so the more compact models likely have a higher appeal as a result.

That said, most units weigh at least 10 pounds, and the weight and size increase quickly with greater capacities. Before purchasing, consider where you plan to store the power bank and the space in your vehicle or camper where it will live while you’re on the road. If you plan to use this power bank solely as a home backup option, portability will matter less, but consider how much effort it will take to move it around within your home or in your outdoor space.

I am a low-maintenance camper, and most of my background is in lightweight backcountry travel. That means I prioritize space-saving and ease-of-use, so my go-to power banks have between 250 and 600 watt-hours, and weigh less than 15 pounds.

This is perfect for a weekend trip, with the on-the-go (car or solar) charging capabilities to put my mind at ease for longer trips. Mostly, I’m charging small items, so one charge lasts a long time. However, plenty of people in the van-life and remote-work world are powering their RVs and vans, and relying on multiple laptop charges. For that, I’d recommend one of the larger units.

A solar-powered generator charges and runs almost anything that requires power—it just depends on the capacity. These generators can charge power tools in the shop, laptops for remote work, and personal devices like Bluetooth headphones and speakers.

A solar-powered generator with a higher power capacity can even power household appliances in the event of a power outage. And the fact that these are solar-compatible means you aren’t reliant on the electrical grid to recharge them.

Every unit on our list has multiple charging options, including wall (AC outlet), car (12-volt), and solar. Each input method charges your unit at a different speed, and solar also depends on the conditions. AC power is the fastest, followed by 12-volt, and then by solar (though a larger solar array could potentially be faster than 12-volt).

I try to charge up my power banks whenever I can, so I’m never caught off guard trying to leave on a trip with a dying power bank. If this happens (which it has), I’ll charge it in my vehicle’s 12-volt port while I’m driving, though this is often slower than solar or a wall unit.

Solar power is the most sustainable and typically fastest way to power these—just be sure you have enough wattage in the solar panels to make it effective. I recommend keeping the generator stored with at least an 80 percent charge, and unplugging it once it’s fully charged—keeping it plugged in longer than necessary degrades the battery.

Most units will have a simple readout display showing the remaining battery charge, and it’s a good practice not to allow your battery pack to get below 20 percent.

David is a Reviews Editor for Hearst’s Enthusiast Group, contributing to Popular Mechanics, Runner’s World, Bicycling, Best Products, and Biography. He has over 25 years of experience writing about and reviewing consumer electronics, kitchen appliances, DIY products, outdoor gear, and more. He also spent years covering the ever-changing world of online retail. To relax, he loves experimenting with new recipes, tweaking his smart home setup, and spending time outdoors on his bike or camping.

#6261. People taking drugs like Ozempic report an unexpected change in their drinking habits

Many people taking GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic reported drinking less alcohol within three months of starting their treatment.

People take Ozempic for many reasons, but cutting back on alcohol is rarely one of them. Yet some patients have noticed a change in their drinking habits after starting the medication.

A national survey of U.S. adults examined changes in drinking habits after people started taking GLP-1 medications.

Among those who drank alcohol before treatment, 44.2% reported drinking less within the first three months.

The change was even more common among people whose drinking habits put them at greater risk of health problems.

The research was led by Lori Uscher-Pines, a distinguished senior research scientist at the Brown University School of Public Health, along with colleagues from several other research institutions.

Ozempic and Wegovy contain semaglutide, a drug that helps regulate blood sugar and appetite. Both belong to a class of medicines called GLP-1 drugs.

Scientists are now exploring whether these medicines might also change how people respond to alcohol.

Early clinical trials have produced encouraging results. One possible explanation involves parts of the brain that control cravings and the sense of pleasure people get from certain activities.

Haiden Huskamp, the Henry J. Kaiser Professor of Health Care Policy at Harvard Medical School, is the study’s senior author.

“Because all of the evidence had been anecdotal when we started this study, it was hard to know what to expect,” said Huskamp.

“But finding that about half of GLP-1 users who drink reported reductions in their alcohol use after starting the medication is pretty striking.”

In March and April 2026, the researchers surveyed members of the RAND American Life Panel, a group of randomly selected adults from across the United States.

Of the 2,857 people invited to participate, 2,009 completed the survey. Their average age was just under 49.

Among the respondents, 368 people had taken a GLP-1 drug at some point. Some were still taking the medication, while others had stopped.

The researchers asked these individuals to think back to their first three months of treatment and describe any changes in their drinking habits.

Not everyone who took these medications drank alcohol. After excluding 126 non-drinkers, the researchers were left with a group of 242 people.

Just over half, 52.6%, noticed no difference in their drinking habits. Another 44.2% said they drank less than before.

Only 3.3% reported an increase in alcohol consumption.

In other words, reports of drinking less were about 13 times as common as reports of drinking more.

The researchers were particularly interested in people whose drinking could put their health at risk.

They used a screening question developed by the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism.

Women were asked how often they had consumed four or more drinks on one occasion during the previous year, while the threshold for men was five drinks.

Across the survey, 37.3% of adults reported at least one such occasion. Among GLP-1 users who met this criterion and drank alcohol, 54.1% reported drinking less after starting treatment.

Another 40.2% noticed no change, while 5.7% said they drank more.

Age, income, sex, race, ethnicity and general health could all potentially influence a person’s relationship with alcohol. The researchers accounted for these factors in their analysis.

Even after doing so, people who screened positive for potentially unhealthy drinking had 2.3 times the odds of reporting a reduction in alcohol consumption.

None of the demographic factors showed a significant association with reporting less drinking.

The findings do not necessarily mean that the drugs work better for heavy drinkers. However, they give researchers a reason to study this particular group more closely.

Ask someone what Ozempic does, and they will probably mention weight loss. Far fewer people appear to know about its possible effects on drinking.

Nearly 80% of survey participants knew that GLP-1 drugs could help people lose weight, and 45.7% knew about their role in blood sugar control.

Yet only 9.7% had heard that these medicines might reduce the desire to drink alcohol. Awareness was somewhat higher among people with potentially unhealthy drinking habits.

Uscher-Pines expects public interest to grow as more research becomes available. Greater demand could also raise questions about insurance coverage and access to prescriptions through telehealth services.

Excessive alcohol consumption contributes to about 178,000 deaths in the United States every year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

For some people, drinking less is not simply a matter of deciding to stop. Alcohol use disorder is a medical condition that makes it difficult to control drinking, even when it causes serious problems.

Medications already exist to help people manage this condition. However, many of those who need help never receive it.

Alisa Busch, a professor of psychiatry at Harvard Medical School, was also involved in the study.

“The national surveys show that far and away most people with alcohol-use disorder receive no treatment, period,” said Busch.

There is a considerable difference between asking people whether they drink less and proving that a medication helps them do so.

“We weren’t testing GLP-1s for efficacy in reducing alcohol use. We’d need a randomized control trial for that,” Busch said.

“We were trying to understand, in a population at higher risk for harmful drinking, is there a difference in their experience of drinking alcohol compared to individuals who screen negative.”

Without a controlled experiment, the researchers cannot rule out other reasons for the changes in drinking habits.

People answered questions about something that had already happened. Their memories may not have been entirely accurate, and some participants may have given answers they thought were more socially acceptable.

The researchers also don’t know how much less alcohol people consumed. Someone who skipped an occasional glass of wine and someone who stopped drinking altogether could both have reported a reduction.

Nor does the study tell us whether these changes lasted beyond the first three months of treatment.

Importantly, the screening question identified potentially unhealthy drinking habits rather than diagnosed cases of alcohol use disorder.

Researchers now need to find out whether GLP-1 drugs can produce meaningful and lasting reductions in alcohol consumption.

“If future studies lead to [Food and Drug Administration] approval of GLP-1s to treat alcohol use disorder, this could be a game changer in addiction treatment,” Uscher-Pines said.

“Clinicians we spoke to are very excited about the potential here.”

“The evidence isn’t there, but it will be very interesting to watch over the next couple of years,” Huskamp said. “There are trials underway. I don’t expect it to take too long before more evidence starts coming through.”

For now, GLP-1 drugs are not approved for treating alcohol use disorder. But what patients have noticed while taking these medications may help scientists develop new ways to treat a condition that remains difficult to manage.

The study is published in the journal JAMA Psychiatry.

#6260. Democrats mulling Iran war funding cutoff strategy

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., talks with reporters in the Capitol on Sept. 30. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

A group of prominent Senate Democrats is pushing to use a must-pass spending bill to cut off funding for the Iran war, complicating the path toward a bipartisan deal for averting a partial government shutdown next month.

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Thursday he is working on legislative language ending the war that he wants attached to the next continuing resolution that is needed by Dec. 11, when current funding runs out.

“I know it’s going to be my main push,” he said. “I have to work with colleagues to try to find some language that works. And I’m not there yet, but I’ve told everybody that’s an opportunity.”

Democratic Sens. Michael Bennet of Colorado, Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, Tammy Duckworth of Illinois and independent Bernie Sanders of Vermont released a statement Thursday that they would oppose any deal that does not include “language that restricts the Trump Administration from using appropriated funds to continue his war against Iran.”

“When we vote on appropriations, we intend to fund the government and stop funds for this war,” the senators said. “It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve.”

It is unlikely that Republicans, who are in control of both chambers of Congress until January, not to mention the Oval Office beyond that, would agree to such a deal.

House Appropriations Chairman Tom Cole, R-Okla., said earlier this week that “a Republican Congress is not going to send bills to a Republican president that he's going to veto.”

While ending the war is a top priority of Democrats as they take back power in the new Congress, insisting on doing so this year could lead to a Christmas-time partial government shutdown. If a shutdown starts after Dec. 11, it’s possible it would still be ongoing when Democrats take control of both chambers in January.

But some Democrats appeared to still be weighing how quickly to push for a cutoff of war funding.

Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash, said that whether or not Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth remains in his job, “we’re still going to have language stopping this war.”

She was coy on whether that fight would take place on the anticipated continuing resolution in December or wait until next year when Democrats take back power, saying that lawmakers are “looking at all options.”

Democrats are committed to ending the "reckless and costly war of choice in Iran," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said Thursday. He deferred to House Appropriations ranking member Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., "to see what’s possible in advance of Dec. 11" in talks with the other top appropriators.

"I don’t want to get out ahead of Congresswoman DeLauro, but House Democrats have uniformly opposed providing any additional money to Donald Trump’s war machine. to Pete Hegseth’s war machine, over in the Middle East," Jeffries said.

It’s not clear how long a potential continuing resolution would last, and DeLauro said earlier this week that she wants it to be as short as possible.

The Office of Management and Budget has not yet submitted “anomalies” — changes to the current spending levels to be included in the continuing resolution — to Congress.

The administration is considering options including a stopgap bill that would run through March, sources familiar with the talks said. But no decision on the timing covered by the anomalies has been made.

Aris Folley, Jacob Fulton and Michael Macagnone contributed to this report.

Archaeologists have found the remains of a 2,900-year-old sanctuary on an island mountaintop, where ancient Greeks may have worshipped the goddess Artemis.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The discovery of a 2,900-year-old mountaintop sanctuary on a Mediterranean island shows the ancient Greek veneration for high mountains and their link to the Greek gods, archaeologists say.

The sanctuary was found during new excavations on Euboea, a very large island only about 30 miles (50 kilometers) northeast of Athens. The sanctuary did not include any buildings, such as a temple. Archaeologists think it was used for offerings and feasting by worshippers for hundreds of years, from about the ninth century B.C. until the first or second century A.D., during Imperial Roman times.

"We know that in the ancient Greek world, religious life was not limited to large temples and urban sanctuaries," excavation leader Chloé Chezeaux, an archaeologist at the Swiss School of Archeology in Greece, told Live Science in an email. "There were also many places of worship in the countryside and in the mountains."

Chezeaux led the excavations this year near the summit of Elatias, one of the highest peaks of Mount Olympus on Euboea. It is not, however, the mainland Mount Olympus traditionally regarded as the abode of the Greek gods.

Chezeaux said that her team first spotted signs of the sanctuary during an archaeological survey in 2025. In excavations throughout Greece, "mountaintop sanctuaries are not uncommon," she said. "The problem is that these sanctuaries often left very little archaeological evidence, sometimes with no visible structures at all, which makes them particularly difficult to identify."

Archaeologists found the sanctuary during a survey in 2025 and first excavated it in 2026.

The sanctuary on the Euboean Olympus, however, has yielded "an exceptional concentration of pottery," she said. The earliest is from at least the ninth century B.C., during the early Greek Geometric period — named after the distinctive patterns on ceramics of the time.

"This means that people were coming to this summit over several centuries, perhaps even for more than a thousand years," Chezeaux said.

The sanctuary was used in ancient times mainly by people from the nearby city of Eretria, where the Swiss School of Archaeology is now based.

"Reaching the summit is quite a physical challenge even today," Chezeaux said. "The final part of our ascent involves walking about 3 kilometres [1.8 miles], with an elevation gain of 650 metres [2,130 feet]"

Researchers now reach the summit from the nearest mountain pass in about an hour, but "it's difficult to estimate how long the journey would have taken in antiquity," she said. "Travel conditions were different, we don't know which routes people followed, and … not everyone visiting the sanctuary necessarily came from the city of Eretria."

The effort required to get to the mountaintop is part of the mystery.

"People were willing to devote considerable time and energy to reaching these places, and in our case they seem to have done so over many generations," Chezeaux said. This raised questions of what the mountain meant to worshippers, and why this particular summit remained important for so long, she said.

The immortal Greek gods of ancient myths were said to watch the affairs of mortal humans from their home on the summit of a different Mount Olympus, in a mountain range between the northern Greek regions of Thessaly and Macedonia. The highest mountain in Greece, it stands at over 9,500 feet (2,900 m) high, while the Euboean Olympus is almost 3,800 feet (1,100 m) high, and the Elatias peak on it is about 100 feet (30 m) lower than its highest peak.

The Mount Olympus in northern Greece is the highest of several mountains with that name.

The tradition of the northern Olympus on mainland Greece dates from the poems of Homer and Hesiod, which were written in about the eighth century B.C. But the name Olympus was already widespread for high mountains, and modern Greece has several mountains bearing this name.

Chezeaux said religious ceremonies were often held at the sanctuary high on the Euboean Olympus, as well as at other sites on the island.

"In antiquity, Eretria had a very rich religious life, with sanctuaries both within the city and throughout its territory," Chezeaux said. "Mount Olympus dominates much of the surrounding region, and its prominent position probably played a role in the choice of this location."

High mountains held particular significance for the ancient Greeks, and the journey to reach the sanctuary may have been part of the religious experience, she noted.

The excavation team has yet to find an altar at the sanctuary. While the chief Greek god Zeus is traditionally associated with mountaintops, an inscription at an ancient site in Eretria mentions "Artemis Olympia" — an epithet that suggests the wild nature goddess Artemis was worshipped at the mountaintop sanctuary.

The remains of offerings found in crevices at the site include bones from sheep and goats.

"Several of them show signs of burning, sometimes at very high temperatures," Chezeaux said. "These finds naturally suggest practices involving animal sacrifice and ritual meals, which played an important role in ancient Greek religion."

#6257. A golden bar of stars cuts through the heart of a spiral galaxy

Hubble’s portrait of NGC 4394 shows how a bar of stars fits into a spiral galaxy and offers a rare perspective on the structure of our own Milky Way.

Today’s Image of the Day features a nearly face-on view of the spiral galaxy NGC 4394.

A pale gold bar stretches across the galaxy’s bright core, while thin lanes of dust curve around the center. Farther out, two spiral arms sweep into the dark.

That angle makes the bar easy to spot and gives us something we can only imagine for our own Milky Way: a view down onto the disk, with the center and the spiral arms visible in the same frame.

The European Space Agency released this Hubble Space Telescope image on November 24.

The galaxy lies about 55 million light-years away in the constellation Coma Berenices. Its light was already on its way here long before humans appeared on Earth.

On a clear, dark night, the Milky Way looks like a hazy band across the sky. That band is part of our galaxy’s disk seen from within.

When we look along the disk, stars at many different distances crowd into the same field of view, and dust obscures much of the light coming from the center.

Astronomers have used infrared telescopes such as Spitzer to look through some of that dust and trace the distribution of stars.

Those observations helped establish that our galaxy has a central bar. A face-on view of NGC 4394 makes it easier to picture how such a feature fits into a spiral galaxy.

The angle also makes it easier to follow the dust. In Hubble’s image, narrow dark filaments arc around the core and wind through the disk.

They stand out where they block light from the stars behind them. Farther along the arms, blue and pink knots punctuate the softer glow of the surrounding stars.

A bar may look like a solid feature in a still image, but the stars that make it up are moving around the galaxy.

One way a bar can form is when nearly circular stellar orbits become stretched. If enough of those elongated orbits line up, the combined light from the stars takes on the shape of a bar.

A passing galaxy can disturb a disk through gravity and help set that process in motion. A disk can also become unstable through gravitational interactions among its own stars.

Either way, a feature that spans a large part of the galaxy can emerge from changes in the paths of individual stars.

Once a bar forms, its gravity can help channel gas inward. That matters because gas supplies the raw material for new stars.

A bar can therefore influence where a galaxy builds its next generation of stars, even though the bright feature we see in the image is mostly the light of stars already there.

Hubble first captured NGC 4394 while studying a different galaxy. One instrument was trained on nearby Messier 85 and its star clusters, while another recorded an adjacent patch of sky containing NGC 4394.

Hubble’s team released that earlier image about a decade ago.

The new portrait combines those observations with data from a program studying 40 galaxies. NGC 4394 belongs to the Virgo Cluster, a gathering of more than 1,000 galaxies.

The researchers want to understand how star formation winds down in crowded environments and whether it follows a different course in galaxies with fewer neighbors.

Star clusters give researchers a way to look backward. By comparing how brightly a cluster shines at different wavelengths, astronomers can estimate its age.

A young cluster marks a place where stars formed relatively recently. Older clusters preserve evidence of earlier activity.

Taken together, their ages and locations can help researchers reconstruct where star formation persisted and where it faded.

That gives the specks along the spiral arms a second role in the image. The bar is the feature you can pick out at a glance, and it offers an immediate point of comparison with the Milky Way.

The star clusters are harder to spot. Each one carries a piece of the galaxy’s history, and Hubble can pick them out even though their light has crossed 55 million years of space to reach us.

#6256. This scientist proves which problems computers can’t solve quickly

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

MIT computer scientist Dor Minzer uses math to prove when there’s no computational shortcut. He now guides graduate students through the kinds of problems that drew him to the field.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Dor Minzer remembers sitting in an undergraduate computation class at Tel Aviv University. He was intrigued by his professor and soon found himself pulled into a new world: the mystifying intersection of math and computation, first laid out by Alan Turing during World War II. Working with the professor, Minzer became deeply interested in the limitations of what computers can and can’t do.

“My part is actually to prove not only do I not know how to do it, but I can prove that it’s impossible,” Minzer says. “You have to really be curious.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Minzer’s hard work has paid off. In 2018, he proved a theoretical computer science problem called the 2-to-2 games conjecture. It asks whether computers can efficiently distinguish games where almost all rules can be satisfied from those where almost none can be satisfied, when the rules have a strict structure.

In September, Minzer and his two graduate students at MIT posted a 95-page milestone paper on the unique games conjecture, which builds off the 2-to-2 conjecture. The paper wasn’t quite ready, but they published to get ahead of a press release from OpenAI, describing its proof for the same problem, slated for only days later. It’s a situation that many mathematicians have found themselves in this year as AI companies flood the field with findings at lightning speed.

Minzer says it’s critical to remember that math, and all the research and contemplation behind it, is very human. “It’s a human activity,” he says. “Research is sort of a living organism, a living body.”

Minzer teaches his own students now. Some days, he talks to his class and gets the sense that nobody is paying attention. But other days, he gets a few students that participate. They have ideas, they’re excited, and they remind him of his own days as a graduate student.

“I feel like now I feel like I’m passing the torch,” he says. “Before you have a Ph.D. adviser, you’re like a new person in a dark room. There are infinite places to go. Your Ph.D. adviser is the person that holds your hand and says, ‘Okay, let’s walk here.’”

#6254. Forest birds get more warning about predators when many other bird species live nearby

More bird species meant more alarm calls when a model hawk flew past, and recordings of more species drew bigger crowds of mobbing birds.

When an owl shows up in a forest during daylight hours, the small birds that see it make lots of noise. They gather around the owl and chirp out their calls. Almost immediately, birds of other species hear the calls and come to join the outcry.

A new study of forest birds in eastern China found more of these interspecies callings in places with greater bird species diversity. Joining forces allowed them to make more calls per minute, alerting everyone within earshot of the owl’s presence.

The result suggests that birds in forests that have fewer species may get less predator warnings, leaving them more vulnerable.

Two doctoral students, Agnishikhe Kumar and Jiahao Wu, are the study’s first authors. Both are at Xi’an Jiaotong-Liverpool University in Suzhou, China, and the University of Liverpool.

Kumar and Wu worked with Eben Goodale, the study’s senior author, and with colleagues at Zhejiang University and other institutions in China, France, and the United States. All of the fieldwork took place in forest reserves in China.

Over more than two years, the team worked in ten nature reserves spread along about 1,025 miles (1,650 kilometers) of eastern China, from tropical Hainan to temperate Shaanxi.

Birds make two different kinds of calls about predators. Alarm calls go out when a predator is moving and attacking, and they often send the birds in a flock scattering into thick vegetation.

Mobbing calls are for a predator that isn’t moving, like an owl in daylight. These calls draw other birds toward the caller, and the crowd harasses the predator and can drive it away.

To set off alarm calls, the researchers used a slingshot to fire an 8-inch (20-centimeter) plastic hawk into the air beside mixed flocks of several species.

For mobbing, they put out a painted foam model of a collared owlet, a small owl that can attack birds, and played recordings of its calls.

Each time, they recorded how many species called, how many calls came per minute, and how quickly the first call came. They also measured the range of pitch the calls covered.

In an interview with Earth.com, Goodale credited his two students with the fieldwork. “Yeah, this was a ton of work,” he said. By his count, the total was 1,277 experiments.

Before each owl test, the team counted the bird species at the site. Where they counted more species, more kinds of birds joined the mobbing and more individual birds took part.

The birds at those sites also called at a higher rate, and their calls covered a wider range of pitch.

Pitch range matters because birds respond most to calls of other species that sound like their own. A broader mix of calls should reach more kinds of listeners.

On 41 islands in Thousand Island Lake, a reservoir in Zhejiang Province, the team saw a similar pattern. The number of bird species on those islands goes up with the size of the island.

Alarm calls were far rarer than mobbing calls. The plastic hawk set them off in 79 of 150 flocks.

The flocks that called gave a median of four alarm calls a minute, compared with a median of 52 calls a minute in the owl tests. One highly social species, Huet’s fulvetta, made 60.2% of all the alarm calls.

A bird that calls while a hawk is near may put itself at risk. Goodale told Earth.com the team thought the pattern might not hold for alarm calls, reasoning that “after one species calls, everyone else should eavesdrop on that and remain quiet.”

Instead, in flocks with more species, more kinds of birds gave alarm calls. The calls came at a higher rate and covered a wider range of pitch.

“We think it may be because the initial information may not be reliable,” Goodale said. Other species may need to keep calling, he added, to stress the threat and make sure the warning reaches their own kind.

In Sri Lanka, the authors wrote, the first bird to call in a flock is usually a babbler. That babbler often calls at any large or fast-moving bird, so the later calls of other species help mark a real attack.

The team found no significant link between a flock’s species count and how quickly the first alarm call came.

The hawk and owl tests showed how much calling went on. To learn whether birds of other species made use of it, the team ran an experiment at seven sites on the largest island in the lake.

Through two speakers, the researchers played the mobbing calls of one, two, four, or eight local species and recorded which birds responded. A recording of crickets, played to check that birds weren’t simply reacting to noise, drew no response.

Across 406 trials, recordings with more species drew more kinds of birds and more individuals. The birds that came made more calls, across a wider range of pitch. The increase leveled off as the number of species in the recording went up.

Birds of species that weren’t in the recording were also more likely to call within the first minute when the recording held more species. When the team counted all responding birds together, the first-minute pattern was too weak to rule out chance.

Huet’s fulvetta leads the mixed flocks in the region and often starts the mobbing. Goodale said the team expected it to play an outsized role in spreading information.

The experiment showed little sign of that. The team compared recordings of four species with and without each of the eight birds, across five measures.

In only four of those 40 comparisons was the response stronger when a particular species was included, and the four involved four different species.

All eight species drew relatively similar responses, Goodale said. “It seems birds are responding to the small acoustic differences between species and registering a higher response when they hear more species,” he added.

To test that idea, the team had built each recording two ways. In one version, every recording had 104 calls per minute, however many species were in it. In the other, each species called at its usual rate, so more species meant more calls.

Birds responded more to recordings with more species even when the number of calls stayed the same. The researchers took that as evidence that the variety of calls matters.

On most of the five measures, adding species had a stronger effect when the number of calls rose too. So the amount of calling appears to matter as well.

Goodale said the finding also applies in reverse. In areas with fewer animals because of habitat loss, hunting, or other causes, the animals that remain could be less informed.

Or they could come to rely more on collecting information themselves. When the information is about predators, he said, that could come at great cost.

The authors compared their finding to earlier studies that tied species diversity to pollination, seed dispersal, and pest control, and wrote that it helps justify conservation.

The experiments recorded how birds called and gathered, so they can’t show whether birds in places with more species are caught by predators less often.

Only mobbing calls were tested with recordings, and only on a single island. Earlier experiments elsewhere, which mostly compared one species with two, found weak effects on communication or no difference in response.

The larger scale of this study partly explains its stronger result, the authors wrote.

The same idea could apply to other information, such as where to find food or habitat, and to other animals. The researchers suggested that experiments with the chemical signals of insects and other invertebrates may be particularly useful.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Biology.

Quantinuum's Helios processor achieved a record-low failure rate of just 0.0005%, suggesting fault-tolerant quantum systems may need far fewer qubits than previously thought.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists at Quantinuum say they've set a new record in quantum error correction that brings large-scale, fault-tolerant systems one step closer.

The team claims their 98-qubit quantum system, Helios, demonstrated a failure rate of just 0.0005% in tests of its quantum memory, which is equivalent to an estimated five uncorrectable errors per million rounds of error checking.

This rate bests the previous benchmark set by Google's 105-qubit Willow quantum chip, which demonstrated an estimated 772 uncorrectable errors per million rounds in comparable tests, for an error rate of 0.0772%.

The result brings quantum computing closer to the "megaquop regime," where systems can run over a million operations without encountering an error, the researchers said. They detailed their findings in a study uploaded Oct. 16 to the arXiv preprint server.

In a statement, Robin Blume-Kohout, co-director of Sandia National Laboratories' Quantum Performance Lab, called the achievement "a significant milestone that quantum computing researchers have been working toward for many years."

"A scaled-up version of this system could reach the reliability required for useful fault-tolerant computation at a feasible size — less than a million physical qubits — which improves the outlook for practical quantum computing," added Blume-Kohout, who was not involved in the research.

Preserving the fragile information stored in qubits is one of quantum computing's greatest challenges and presents a major barrier to making systems practical.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Qubits, the most basic units of quantum information, are extremely sensitive to interference. Their delicate quantum states can be easily disturbed by heat, vibrations and other forms of environmental "noise," and if this happens in the middle of a calculation, the result becomes far less reliable — if it survives at all.

Quantum error correction has become a focal point for researchers for this exact reason. It introduces redundancy to quantum systems to ensure that small, potentially manageable errors don't wipe out entire calculations.

This involves spreading quantum information across multiple physical qubits to form a "logical" qubit. If a single qubit loses its quantum state due to interference, the redundancy provided by the logical qubit helps to keep the information it collectively stores intact.

The challenge is packing enough qubits into computers to ensure redundancy for longer, more complex calculations. This presents something of a catch-22: Adding more qubits provides more redundancy, allowing for larger quantum systems, but it also increases the opportunity for errors.

Unlike Google's Willow processor, which is based on superconducting circuits, Helios uses electrically charged barium ions that can be dynamically rearranged.

By shuttling ions around the processor, scientists can unite different pairs of qubits, allowing them to exchange information directly. That way, it doesn't have to pass through multiple qubits — a process that can introduce additional errors.

The team also developed a technique called "leakage repumping," which uses precise, split-second laser pulses to bring qubits that have slipped out of their information-storing quantum state back into a usable state.

To test how effectively Helios could correct errors as more physical qubits were added, the researchers used a type of error-correcting code known as a color code. They tested three progressively larger versions ‪—‬ known as code distances 3, 5 and 7 ​​—‬ which could correct one, two and three physical-qubit errors, respectively.

They found that Helios became substantially more reliable as they added more physical qubits. Each increase in code distance reduced the likelihood of an uncorrectable error by roughly 12 times. At the highest level tested (distance 7), Helios achieved a record failure rate of approximately one uncorrectable error per 200,000 rounds.

In the study, which has not been peer-reviewed yet, the scientists suggested that future quantum computers using the same technology as Helios could achieve extremely low error rates without needing an impractically high number of physical qubits.

According to estimates from Quantinuum representatives, a future trapped-ion system could support 100 logical qubits using approximately 30,000 physical qubits, compared with around 900,000 for a competing superconducting system.

"There is still substantial engineering ahead to scale to much larger systems and integrate all the elements of fault-tolerant computation, but this work demonstrates that our underlying hardware and error-correction approach can deliver the exponential improvement in reliability that large-scale quantum computers will depend upon," Dave Hayes, director of computational design and theory at Quantinuum, told Live Science in an email.

The researchers said they plan to apply their latest findings to Quantinuum's upcoming quantum

#6252. Van Hollen announces bid for majority leader, but Schumer says he has the votes

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., left, has announced a challenge to current Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo)

Sen. Chris Van Hollen announced Thursday night that he would run for Senate majority leader, launching a challenge to Sen. Charles E. Schumer of New York, the current Democratic leader.

Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat first elected to the Senate in 2016, served in leadership in the House and has been chairman of both the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. He has said since the midterm elections he was listening to fellow Senate Democrats about the possibility of a run for the top job.

“In this election, the American people called for change. They called for a change from Donald Trump’s disastrous policies but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn’t working for working people,” Van Hollen said in a statement. “It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership. This is not about any one person – it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.”

Schumer has already said he has the votes needed to continue serving as the leader.

“I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead. I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader. I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people,” Schumer said in a statement.

Schumer's supporters were quick to highlight the success at the ballot box in 2026, with the Democratic caucus potentially growing to 56 seats if former Rep. Mary Peltola prevails in Alaska.

“Chuck has outlined an aggressive plan for the new Democratic majority which is directly responsive to the message we heard from the voters, and he has the experience and unique mastery of the Senate process to make it happen,” Sen. Angus King, a Maine independent who caucuses with the Democrats, said in a statement. “Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?”

In keeping with the World Series theme, Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., echoed King with her own statement of support for Schumer.

“The Brewers just had a record season, and next year is not the time to change our management," Baldwin said. "The same is true in the Senate.”

In an interview with MS NOW about his run, Van Hollen conceded that Schumer would be the favorite in the secret-ballot contest, which will take place in December.

“Am I the underdog? Yes,” Van Hollen said. “You’re talking about an incumbent who uses the power of incumbency to, you know, provide deals to people.”

Van Hollen outlined legislative priorities including restoring Medicaid funding that Republicans cut in last year's budget reconciliation law and extending Affordable Care Act tax credits. But he suggested Democrats need to go further.

"We need to extend tax credits for the Affordable Care Act, but we can’t stop there, right? We have a completely broken health care system. It’s become profits, not people. And so my view is, we also need in the first 100 days to make health care more affordable for tens of millions of people," Van Hollen said. "We need to immediately make it clear that nobody’s going to pay one penny to subsidize data centers. ... We need to make sure that we have a livable minimum wage."

He also said he would not take sides in contested Democratic primaries, and he would make sure the DSCC did not take money from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC.

Van Hollen's early backers include progressive Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who emerged from a hotly contested Democratic primary in Michigan while the Senate Democratic political apparatus was backing Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich.

“In April, I was the first candidate in the country to call on Senator Chris Van Hollen to lead Senate Democrats, and I am proud to stand with him in his bid to become Senate Majority Leader,” El-Sayed said in a statement. “Michiganders demand money out of politics, money in pockets, and Medicare for All. Sen. Chris Van Hollen offers both the courage to go toe-to-toe with the Trump administration to deliver for working people and the experience to maneuver the Senate caucus. It’s why he has my full support to lead our caucus.”

#6251. Countries clash over fossil fuels as COP31 ends without a major climate deal

COP31 ended without a major climate agreement after countries clashed over fossil fuels, emissions cuts and climate funding.

The final draft of the main agreement at this year’s UN climate summit had one glaring omission. Nowhere in the document did the words fossil fuels appear.

Several countries rejected it for that reason.

COP31 ended on Sunday, November 22, in Antalya, Türkiye. The talks lasted two weeks and then ran two more days. That made it the longest UN climate summit on record.

Governments still did not agree on the main text.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres called the outcome “deeply disappointing.”

“There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science,” Guterres said in a statement.

Murat Kurum, Türkiye’s environment minister, was the president of COP31. He had little good news at the end of the summit.

“I understand that there is no agreement on this text. For that reason, these decisions have not been adopted,” Kurum said.

Australia led the negotiations. For several days it worked with Türkiye on new versions of the agreement. Both countries tried to find language that everyone could accept.

Some countries wanted a firm commitment to use less coal, oil and gas. Countries that sell fossil fuels abroad worried about what that would mean for their economies.

The proposed text said the world is heading for more than 2.7°F (1.5°C) of warming.

Under the Paris Agreement, governments agreed to hold warming well below 2°C above preindustrial levels and pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C.

The text also asked for more technology to remove carbon dioxide from the air. It said nothing about burning less fossil fuel in the first place.

The European Union would not accept an agreement that avoided the subject. The bloc described the omission as “unconscionable.”

Panama had sent a letter to the summit presidency with its priorities. Its delegation said governments had a responsibility “not to negotiate the minimum threshold, but to act.”

In the Marshall Islands, where much of the land lies just above sea level, the stakes are particularly high.

Accepting the deal, the country’s delegation said, would mean betraying its own people. It rejected what it called “false solutions” and pushed for a faster, adequately funded shift away from fossil fuels.

Speaking for the African Group, Ghana raised concerns about climate funding and financial assistance for countries suffering climate damage.

There was also the question of how to support workers and communities as fossil fuel industries decline.

That issue got “a single generic sentence,” according to Ghana.

Nevertheless, the African Group chose not to block the deal, acknowledging that the text reflected the views of many countries.

Saudi Arabia saw things differently. Speaking for the League of Arab States, it defended keeping carbon capture and storage in the agreement.

This technology traps carbon dioxide and stores it before it reaches the atmosphere.

Was this simply greenwashing? Saudi Arabia argued otherwise, pointing to scientific assessments that give carbon capture a role in limiting global warming.

Pakistan urged countries to keep talking. Its delegation said climate action needs “bridges, not barriers.”

Part of the frustration at COP31 goes back three years.

At the 2023 climate summit in Dubai, governments agreed to transition away from fossil fuels. Guterres said countries now need to speed up that transition and pay for it.

“We can’t put out the fire while pouring fuel on it,” he said.

Guterres also blamed powerful fossil fuel interests for holding back climate action while they keep making profits.

He wants deeper emissions cuts before 2030. He also wants more money for vulnerable countries to cope with climate change.

Not everything fell apart in Antalya. Governments agreed on several smaller decisions.

Simon Stiell, the head of UN Climate Change, pointed to progress on the just transition.

Picture a town where hundreds of families depend on a coal mine. When the mine closes, those families need help. A just transition means supporting workers and communities through changes like that.

Governments will continue their work on the issue for three more years. They will also set up a mechanism in stages. Plans for it were first agreed at last year’s summit in Belém, and formal adoption is expected at COP32.

Countries that make up about half of the world economy backed a goal of 35% electrification by 2035.

In practice, that means more cars, heating systems and factory machines running on electricity instead of burning fuel.

The International Energy Agency estimates the pledge could raise the global electrification rate from 23% to more than 33% by 2035.

Stiell said progress like this could help bring about positive tipping points in climate action.

Tropical rainforests got some good news too. Pledges to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility, which helps protect these forests, reached $8.3 billion.

Stiell talked openly about what went wrong in Antalya in his closing remarks. “The world cannot afford a repeat of this moment,” he said.

He also spoke about how governments make decisions at these summits.

“This process belongs to 194 Parties. Consensus works best from the ground up,” Stiell said.

Next year, Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, will host the climate talks. Countries will pick up where they left off in Türkiye.

There is still no agreement on how quickly the world should move away from coal, oil and gas. For poorer nations, another problem remains: who will pay for the transition?

#6250. In 1935, crews dangled from cliffs to build a Grand Canyon phone line, now the Park Service wants to its copper wire

Hanging wires in the inner canyon put helicopter and emergency operations and wildlife at risk. The Park Service says removing some would be an adverse effect on a listed historic line.

In the 1934-35 season, Civilian Conservation Corps crews built a telephone line down into the Grand Canyon and up the other side, according to a National Park Service history page. Workers often had to dangle from ropes on the cliffs to set poles into the rock.

The line connected the North and South rims in 1935. It gave the two rims instantaneous communication, though it could handle only one call at a time, according to the park.

More than 90 years later, the Park Service has proposed removing sections of the line’s wire. Its original copper wire, now hanging or lying in places across the inner canyon, has become a hazard for helicopter and emergency operations and for wildlife.

The Trans-Canyon Telephone Line runs through the inner canyon, generally following the Bright Angel and North Kaibab trails, with a spur toward the South Kaibab Trail.

It was strung from tree to rock, the park says, and it was frequently out of commission. While the park’s history page says the CCC built the line, the agency’s newest notice describes it as “reconstructed by Civilian Conservation Corps crews in 1935.”

The Civilian Conservation Corps was created in 1933, when President Franklin Delano Roosevelt signed the law that set it up. The program gave poor, unemployed young men work on conservation projects across the country’s public lands.

At the Grand Canyon, its crews built trails, walls and shelters, and they helped the park put in roads, campgrounds and telephone lines. The program ended in 1942.

Today the line is listed in the National Register of Historic Places for its importance to the park’s communications, engineering and administrative history.

But according to the Park Service, suspended, hanging and fallen telephone wires have created risks to helicopter and emergency operations in the inner canyon. They can also pose entanglement hazards for wildlife.

Under the proposal, the park would remove sections of the historic wire where necessary to eliminate those hazards. On the wire it keeps, it would add visibility markers where appropriate.

The historic poles, cross-arms, insulators and other hardware would stay in place, unless one of them presents a safety hazard of its own.

The plan is still a proposal, not finished work. The park took public comments for 15 days, from October 28 until midnight on November 11, 2026, and that comment period has now closed.

The Park Service acknowledges a cost to the historic line. Because the original copper wire is an important historic feature of the line, removing portions of it and adding markers “would alter characteristics that contribute to the property’s historical significance,” the agency said.

Under the National Historic Preservation Act, it added, “those changes are considered an adverse effect.”

To deal with that, the park worked with Arizona’s State Historic Preservation Officer on a draft Memorandum of Agreement.

According to the Park Service, the agreement would let the park address known safety hazards while documenting and preserving the history and significance of the telephone line.

The telephone line is one of many pieces of the Grand Canyon that date to that era. Hikers on the Bright Angel Trail still use resthouses built by the CCC, and Bright Angel Campground sits on the site of the corps’ camp at Phantom Ranch, the park says.

Elsewhere in the park, the South Rim hotels reopened 81 days after a deadly flood, which echoed a disaster in 1966.

The canyon’s rocks hold a far older record. Geologists have found fossils of unexpected creatures in the Grand Canyon’s Bright Angel Formation.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service news release Grand Canyon National Park Seeks Public Comment on Trans-Canyon Telephone Line (October 28, 2026) and the Grand Canyon National Park history pages Building the National Park and Civilian Conservation Corps.

#6248. Astronomer Isabel Angelo hunts for odd signals in telescope data

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A comet or a newborn star might explain an odd signal in telescope data. Astrophysicist Isabel Angelo is looking for signals that defy those familiar explanations.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Isabel Angelo spends her days searching the cosmos for exoplanets and signs of extraterrestrial intelligence. But Angelo’s head isn’t in the stars. It’s buried under mountains of 0s and 1s — data from space telescopes old and new.

To piece together a fuller picture of what’s out there (alien megastructures around nearby stars, perhaps?), Angelo and her colleagues at the SETI Institute in Mountain View, Calif., are turning to machine learning models. These tools are analyzing the troves of telescope data for anomalies — things that look “weird” in space that we don’t know how to explain yet.

Most of the space weirdos will probably turn out to be total normies — a comet, a newborn star or a star surrounded by lots of gas and dust. “These are things that I would expect [the models] to find,” Angelo says. “But the goal is to find something that’s not even in any of these categories.”

In the meantime, Angelo keeps her whimsy and wonder for space alive by remembering historic moments, like the reveal of the first portrait of a black hole in 2019. The scientists “put all of these telescopes all over the Earth. They wait for the Earth to rotate. They do all this math to construct this one image,” Angelo says. “I can’t believe how creative and innovative we have to be to learn about space. It’s such a specific and really fun challenge.”
