#6247. Oceanfront structures in Rodanthe could collapse during a storm forecast for North Carolina’s Outer Banks on November 25 and 26, the Park Service warns

Damaged septic systems could expose waste on Rodanthe beaches, and drivers should avoid vulnerable parts of N.C. Highway 12 at high tide.

People on North Carolina’s Outer Banks should stay out of the ocean, avoid driving on the beach and avoid vulnerable sections of N.C. Highway 12 at high tide on November 25 and 26, according to the National Park Service.

A coastal storm is forecast to bring strong, gusty winds and elevated water levels to Cape Hatteras National Seashore on those two days.

In the village of Rodanthe, threatened oceanfront structures “could partially or completely collapse,” the Park Service warned on November 24.

This is a warning, not a report of damage. But the seashore says the risk goes beyond the structures themselves.

Damaged septic systems could expose waste, the Park Service said, “creating serious hazards for people walking on the beach or wading nearby.”

Most off-road vehicle routes on the beach will likely be impassable during the storm, according to the seashore, and hazardous surf will make swimming unsafe. Visitors should avoid beach driving and stay out of the water until conditions improve.

N.C. Highway 12, the main road along the islands, is also at risk. The Park Service says travelers should avoid its vulnerable sections during high tides on November 25 and 26, and that hazardous weather may cause road closures.

It lists four areas where driving may be very difficult during the storm:

On Ocracoke Island, a two-mile stretch of highway south of off-road vehicle ramp 59.

On southern Hatteras Island, the road between the villages of Hatteras and Frisco.

On central Hatteras Island, the area along the northern boundary of Buxton.

On northern Hatteras Island, the road between the Pea Island Visitor Center and the Basnight Bridge, as well as side streets in northern Rodanthe.

All of the seashore’s campgrounds remain open, the Park Service says, but minor flooding and strong wind gusts will make for unfavorable camping conditions.

It points travelers to the National Weather Service at weather.gov/mhx for forecasts and to the North Carolina Department of Transportation at drivenc.gov for road conditions.

The seashore has issued similar warnings in 2026.

On April 7, it urged visitors to use caution on east-facing beaches through April 11. The potential for multi-day, persistent northeast winds and breaking waves, it said, could cause coastal erosion and “the partial or full collapse of one or more threatened oceanfront structures in Buxton and Rodanthe.”

At that time, the entire beach in front of Buxton was closed because of hazards from threatened oceanfront structures “in or near the ocean,” according to the Park Service.

After a recent coastal storm, the seashore reported significant impacts in a September 28 update. It said Dare County had declared a state of emergency for Hatteras Island, and non-resident travel to the island was prohibited.

The Avon Fishing Pier had an estimated 20-foot gap in its structure. The beach was closed from the northern boundary of Rodanthe to the pier in Rodanthe, and people were told to avoid the ocean because of possible poor water quality from damaged septic systems.

Private beach stairs and boardwalk decking, septic system parts, and wooden and metal debris from houses were littering the beach, the Park Service said at the time.

Cape Hatteras National Seashore sits on barrier islands, and those islands are not fixed in place. One study predicts that barrier islands will retreat faster than they have in the past, and healthy dunes help protect the coasts behind them when storms hit.

The Park Service’s advice for now is practical: use caution on the beach, avoid beach driving and stay out of the water during the storm, and check road conditions before driving N.C. Highway 12.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service news releases Cape Hatteras National Seashore Warns of Hazardous Conditions and Threatened Structures During Coastal Storm (November 24, 2026), Cape Hatteras National Seashore Reports Status Updates After Recent Coastal Storm (September 28, 2026) and Cape Hatteras National Seashore Urges Caution Near Threatened Oceanfront Structures in Buxton and Rodanthe (April 7, 2026).

On Wednesday (Nov. 25), the distant ice giant Uranus will be at its best and brightest. Here's when, where and how to look for the seventh planet.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

One of the hardest planets to see in the solar system — the distant ice giant Uranus — reaches its annual opposition on Wednesday (Nov. 25), just a day after the Beaver Supermoon. It's the best time to see the seventh planet from the sun, but you'll need to use stargazing binoculars or a good backyard telescope to find it.

Uranus is faint, slow-moving and rarely a target for casual stargazers. However, on Nov. 25, and, for a few weeks on either side, it will be at its closest point to Earth this year and will appear at its brightest, making it possible to spot.

Opposition occurs when Earth passes between Uranus and the sun; Uranus will be "opposite" the sun, hence, "opposition." The moment of opposition will happen at 6 p.m. ET on Nov. 25, according to EarthSky. Consequently, Uranus will rise in the east around sunset, reach its highest point in the sky around midnight and set in the west around sunrise.

You can find it in the constellation Taurus, close to the Pleiades open star cluster, also known as the Seven Sisters and M45. Uranus will be a few degrees southeast of the cluster, appearing as a faint point of light, about two-fifths of the distance between the Pleiades and Aldebaran, the brightest star in Taurus.

At magnitude +5.6, Uranus is technically visible to the naked eye under very dark skies. However, binoculars or a telescope will make it much easier to find.

Uranus as seen by NASA's Hubble Space Telescope.

At opposition, Uranus will be 18.4 astronomical units (AU) from Earth — about 1.7 billion miles (2.7 billion kilometers) away. Through a telescope, it will appear as a tiny blue-green disk. Its color comes from methane in its atmosphere, which absorbs red wavelengths of sunlight.

Named after Ouranos, the ancient Greek god of the sky and the heavens, according to the Planetary Society , Uranus is one of the least understood planets in the solar system. A day on Uranus lasts for about 17 hours, and the planet rotates sideways, according to NASA. It takes 84 Earth years to orbit the sun.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Uranus also has 13 faint rings and at least 29 known moons, the most recent of which was found in 2025 by the James Webb Space Telescope. It was named Uranus XXVIII and orbits between the moons Ophelia and Bianca. Many of Uranus' moons are named after characters from the works of William Shakespeare and Alexander Pope.

The distant planet has been visited only once, by NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft on Jan. 24, 1986. However, contrary to what the probe found, scientists now think the planet emits its own internal heat. That could increase pressure on NASA to prepare a Uranus Orbiter and Probe (UOP), a mission concept the National Academy of Sciences recommended in 2022 as a high-priority planetary science mission for the next decade.

Uranus will next come to opposition on Nov. 30, 2027.

#6245. Calls for Nvidia probes, new chip export limits intensify

“The bottom line is we need to understand the magnitude of this with respect to Chinese intelligence, possible chip diversion,” said Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., seen above. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo)

The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday did little to quell bipartisan demands from Congress for an accounting of potential national security fallout from his affair with an alleged Chinese spy and talk of adding tougher chip export controls to the annual defense authorization bill.

Huang admitted on Sunday to having an affair, and reports say that it was with Alice Huang, an executive at Singaporean tech company and Nvidia customer Megaspeed, whom the U.S. government believes spied for China, according to recent reports. The New York Times and Reuters reported he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters Thursday that he supports the Senate investigating Huang’s potential influence on U.S. artificial intelligence and chip policy.

“I think that it would make sense because of the… nature of the association… and the governments and the national security interests we were talking about here,” Thune said, though he said he thought it would be “wrong” to make assumptions about how close Huang’s relationship with President Donald Trump has been.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., echoed the need for lawmakers to delve into the scandal, saying in a post on X that “Congress must demand answers.”

“The Trump administration must also answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Were government officials told not to investigate because of Trump’s relationship with Mr. Huang? What did Trump know when he personally invited Mr. Huang aboard Air Force One?” Schumer wrote, referring to the president having invited Huang to accompany him to China in May.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said at a press conference that Reps. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., and Jim Himes, D-Conn., the ranking members of the Foreign Affairs and Intelligence committees, respectively, are leading Democrats’ efforts to “get to the bottom of what has happened.”

“We need a classified briefing made available to members of Congress as it relates to the Nvidia situation,” Jeffries said. “And to the extent that our national security has been compromised, the American people deserve answers, and we're going to work to make sure that happens.”

The investigations look likely to begin before control of Congress changes hands in January.

Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., who chairs the House select China committee, told reporters that his panel, along with House Foreign Affairs and Intelligence, are in negotiations with Huang to find a date for his testimony before Congress.

“The bottom line is we need to understand the magnitude of this with respect to Chinese intelligence, possible chip diversion,” Moolenaar said. “What ways is Chinese intelligence influencing his perspective, his perspective influencing national security policy?”

Last week, the chairs of the three committees sent a letter to Huang requesting that he appear at a joint closed-door briefing. Moolenaar said that if Huang does not agree to a date, the committees will subpoena him.

Late Thursday, he joined with House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., and House Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford, R-Ark., in sending a new letter to Huang seeking a closed-door transcribed interview on Dec. 1. They also wrote to Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter seeking a similar interview on Dec. 2. Separately, Mast wrote to Jeffrey Kessler, the Commerce Department undersecretary for industry and security, seeking his appearance at a committee hearing on Dec. 3.

Moolenaar also said that Congress needs to understand what privileged information Chinese intelligence may have gained access to through Huang and how they may have tried to influence U.S. policy.

“We need to have strong safeguards when it comes to our technology and export controls,” Moolenaar said. “And [Huang has] been one of the strongest proponents for not having export controls. This shines a whole new light on that discussion.”

Also late Thursday, Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C.,  sent a letter to Huang calling on him to appear at a Dec. 3 committee hearing and another letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify at a Dec. 10 hearing "regarding recent public reports about NVIDIA and the Department of Commerce's role that raises national security concerns."

A proposed manager’s amendment to the Senate's fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill (S 4784) contains several possibilities for those safeguards, including requirements for chip security mechanisms that would allow for verification if semiconductors are diverted to countries of concern and a ban on exporting certain very powerful chips to those countries. The House NDAA does not contain similar language.

However, House Armed Services Chair Mike D. Rogers, D-Ala., is open to the restrictions. He told reporters Wednesday that he “would like to see” semiconductor export controls in the NDAA, but that the Huang scandal had not changed his position.

Democratic Caucus Vice Chair Ted Lieu, D-Calif., told reporters on Thursday that after reports that the federal government had been aware of Huang’s affair with the alleged spy, the administration should have shared the information with Congress.

“The administration needs to be investigated for hiding this information from Congress and the American people,” he said.

Lieu also suggested that Nvidia’s reported donation to the White House ballroom project influenced the Trump administration’s decision to allow the export of some powerful Nvidia chips to China.

“There is no reason to do that. That hurts our national security, and we have an opportunity right now to fix that in the upcoming National Defense Authorization,” Lieu said.

Mast said the Huang revelations could give new momentum to including chip export rules in the NDAA. He also said that his “directive” on the issue came “straight from the admin” and informed his objectives on the committee.

“Don't let chips be smuggled to China. Make sure that American companies get to buy them first,” Mast said. “Make sure that the machines that make them don't get sold to them, even though it's the Dutch that make the machines. Make sure that they can't access it remotely.”

Mast’s committee has advanced many of those priorities, including some of the language included in the NDAA.

In March, the committee on a unanimous vote advanced legislation known as the Chip Security Act, which would require chip security mechanisms to verify that certain semiconductors subject to export controls aren’t diverted to countries of concern, including China and Iran.

The committee also advanced bills to require the Bureau of Industry and Security and the State Department to work with allied suppliers of semiconductor manufacturing equipment to implement export controls to prevent the equipment from going to countries of concern, and to require licenses for the export of certain powerful chips, including banning exporting certain chips to countries of concern.

Versions of all three bills are included in the Senate manager’s amendment to the NDAA.

The scandal has also led to calls for oversight of the Commerce Department, including Secretary Howard Lutnick, for its handling of export policy and actions around Huang.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters Thursday that Lutnick and Nvidia should testify “before Democrats can set the narrative.”

“If there is some reasonable basis or some way to discount some of the reporting, the best way to do it is request a meeting with us and give us a briefing,” Tillis said. “Because otherwise, you're going to get what you get in an oversight hearing in about six weeks.”

Asked about oversight of the Commerce Department’s role in the Huang scandal, Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, who chairs the Commerce Committee, said his panel “has engaged in vigorous oversight under Republican presidents and Democrat presidents and will continue to be [engaged in it].”

On Wednesday, prior to Huang’s resignation, Senate Banking ranking member Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller requesting that they “preserve all documents, communications, records, and other materials regarding the export of NVIDIA’s advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China.”

“This incident raises significant concerns about the federal government’s ability to effectively enforce our export controls and protect our national security,” the senators wrote.

In a statement Thursday, Warren said that Huang’s resignation did not “absolve” him of the need to answer questions. She also called for the passage of stricter export controls, including the bill to ban the export of certain chips to China.

Sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., sent his own letter on Wednesday to Lutnick, Rubio, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, requesting an update on the Justice Department’s investigation into Megaspeed for possibly diverting U.S. chips to China.

Savannah Behrmann, John M. Donnelly, Jacob Fulton and David Jordan contributed to this report.

#6244. Why do some memories stick for years? A teenager’s extraordinary memory offers a clue

A teenager with highly superior autobiographical memory tests like anyone else, but her own past returns uninvited at least once a day.

Give a teenager from the Atlanta area a date from years ago, and she can tell you what day of the week it was, what she wore, or what the weather was like. Yet her scores on standard memory tests were typical.

In a new case report, the teenager said memories of her past came back on their own at least daily. Adults in an earlier survey reported that happening about once a week on average.

The condition is called highly superior autobiographical memory, or HSAM, and it was first described in 2006.

Psychologist Anne Cleary of Colorado State University and neuroscientist Daniel Drane, then at Emory University, examined the teenager in June 2024.

They report on her as a single case, so the pattern they found still has to hold up in other people.

“It seems as if people with HSAM are reliving these past experiences more frequently and that strengthens the memories overall, making memories more stable over time for them,” Cleary said.

For years, she added, researchers had speculated that people with HSAM might be better at deliberately retrieving memories, “but our work seems to show the crucial difference lies in how often memories return on their own.”

Her parents had noticed that her memory for her own life was unusually strong, and a colleague at Johns Hopkins University sent the family to Drane.

She was 16 when Cleary and Drane sat down with her and her mother at Emory. They read out dates, some chosen in advance and some made up on the spot, then holidays, then family trips: 14 prompts in all.

She answered so fast that the researchers paused after the first date to set up a video camera.

“Give me a date and I will tell you everything that happened on that day,” she told them. “What I did, what I was wearing, what happened that day.”

The first date was November 5, 2021. She said it was a Friday, and that school was out because the Atlanta Braves were holding their World Series parade. It was overcast, she said, and the sunset that evening was unusually pretty.

Cleary checked afterward. A local news story confirmed the school closure, a weather archive confirmed the clouds, and a dated photo posted online showed the sunset.

Every one of the 14 prompts produced details that held up the same way, including the day of the week.

The girl also sat through a standard battery of memory and thinking tests, and her results were unremarkable. That matches what researchers have reported since the first HSAM case 20 years ago.

People with the condition recall their own lives in extraordinary detail, yet they perform about like anyone else when asked to memorize a list of words.

Cleary’s team thinks the reason is what those tests measure.

Most of them ask a person to remember on purpose. Asked whether her own recall took effort, the girl said she could do it by strategy, “but usually it just sort of happens, just naturally.”

So the team gave her a questionnaire built for the other kind of remembering. These are the memories that arrive uninvited while a person is doing something else, which psychologists call involuntary memories.

Earlier descriptions had hinted that people with HSAM get more of them. But Cleary’s team says no one had directly measured how often they happen in a person with the condition.

The questionnaire has 20 items. Ten ask how often memories of the past pop up on their own, and ten ask the same about thoughts of the future.

Each answer is one of five steps: never, once a month, once a week, once a day, or once an hour or more.

On the past-oriented items, the teenager’s average answer landed between once a day and once an hour. When the same questionnaire was given to 200 adults in a 2015 study, the average answer was about once a week.

Her score was just over two standard deviations above that group’s mean, a gap the researchers call significantly higher than typical. Her future-oriented thoughts were more frequent than average too, though by less.

The team builds its proposal on that gap. Each time a memory comes back, she relives it, and the researchers propose that all those unplanned replays are what makes her memories so durable.

They present it as a hypothesis the case supports, not as proof.

The team looked at one more thing, and it didn’t stand out.

Some researchers argue that déjà vu and involuntary memories come from the same mechanism, with déjà vu as the faint version, a memory stirred but not quite retrieved.

A 2026 study found that people who report more involuntary memories also report more déjà vu.

The researchers asked whether she also experienced déjà vu more often than usual.

She chose “a few times per year,” the most common answer among college students who had taken the same questionnaire.

Her mental imagery didn’t stand out either. On a standard vividness questionnaire she scored 58. People with typical imagery average about 57 on it, and people with unusually vivid mental pictures average about 78.

Whatever sets her apart, then, it isn’t a sharper mind’s eye. On questionnaires about inner speech and the kinds of images she thinks in, she also scored inside the ordinary range.

One person can’t show how common this pattern is. The questionnaire relies on the very thing it’s trying to measure, a person’s memory of her own experiences.

So the researchers want future studies to catch involuntary memories as they happen, with prompts during the day.

Her age limited the testing. The quiz about public events that earlier HSAM studies used was built for adults, and a teenage version didn’t work either, because she doesn’t follow the news.

A June 2026 preprint from another group used both the questionnaire and real-time prompts on a 16-year-old boy with HSAM and found more involuntary memories either way.

Drane, now at The Ohio State University, said the teenager has since completed an MRI of her brain and other experimental tasks “which will be the subject of future work.”

Cleary said the case could help build better memory tests. One use is for epilepsy surgery patients whose families notice something missing even when standard tests come back clean.

Whether those daily returns are what keeps her memories so durable is still untested.

Tracking involuntary memories as they happen in more people with HSAM could show how common the pattern is.

The full study was published in the journal Neurocase.

#6243. Motion under the ocean explains the depth of the world’s deepest spot

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A tight bend in the subducting Pacific plate may help explain Challenger Deep

The ROV Jason/Medea (Jason shown here during a 2021 dive at the East Pacific Rise) can descend up to 6,500 meters below the ocean surface. In a new study, it helped researchers discover volcanic deposits in the Mariana Trench.

D. Fornari, WHOI-SSSG, MISO Facility, NDSF Jason Team, NSF

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Challenger Deep is the deepest valley in the deepest trench in the ocean, plunging to roughly 11,000 meters below sea level.

Now, scientists have a new clue about how it got to be so … well, deep.

Challenger Deep is found within the Mariana Trench, a crescent-shaped gouge in the seafloor east of the Philippines in the Pacific Ocean. The trench is the scene of a slo-mo tectonic collision called a subduction zone: The Pacific plate is diving beneath the Mariana plate, bending downward as it sinks into the mantle, forming a steep trench on the ocean floor.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

All subduction zones are deep, but “it’s interesting why this is the deepest spot in the Earth’s ocean,” says geoscientist Robert Stern, an emeritus professor at the University of Texas at Dallas and a visiting researcher at the University of California, Los Angeles.

He and colleagues employed a remotely operated robot called ROV Jason/Medea to descend to more than 6,000 meters and explore the Mariana Trench seafloor around the edges of Challenger Deep. The rocks turned out to contain pyroclastic deposits, evidence of an erstwhile explosive volcanic eruption. Those deposits included platelike blocks that could indicate eruption pulses, and lobe-shaped rocks where the volcanic flows ended and quickly cooled.

These are the deepest pyroclastic deposits found on Earth, the scientists report November 23 in Frontiers in Earth Science.

How explosive an eruption is at Earth’s surface depends on the chemical makeup of the magma. When the molten rock contains a high proportion of volatile gases, including water vapor, those gases suddenly expand when the magma reaches the surface, producing a violent explosion.

Such explosive volcanism shouldn’t be possible in the deep sea; the pressure is too high for any escaping gases to expand, Stern says. Along with that mystery, the volcanic deposits were found unusually close to the trench, compared with what would be expected for a subduction zone.

Stern and his colleagues developed a hypothesis that incorporates these disparate pieces of evidence: The extreme depth of Challenger Deep, they say, may be at least partially due to an especially sharp bend in the Pacific Plate as it sinks into the mantle.

That tighter bend would explain why volcanism is happening closer to the subduction zone than usual. The classic subduction zone scenario is that the sinking plate heats up and melts partially as it descends; the magma rises through the overhanging plate and erupts, forming volcanic island arcs several hundred kilometers from the collision zone. Here, the volcanic deposits were just a hundred kilometers or so from the trench — which makes sense if the plate is dipping more steeply.

As for the pyroclastics, “we can’t answer if the eruptions were really explosive,” Stern says. But at those pressures, any gases such as water vapor contained in the magma wouldn’t be able to explosively expand as they would at the surface.

Instead, the pyroclastic rocks might have formed through a new version of deep-sea eruption, one in which water emerging from the magma is initially in a supercritical fluid state. That would minimize any explosive expansion during the eruption and could also produce fragmented, dense deposits like those seen by Jason/Medea.

The discovery of deep-sea pyroclastics is “surprising and unprecedented,” says William Chadwick, a geologist at Oregon State University in Newport. Challenger Deep may be the only place on Earth “with the ingredients to produce explosive volcanism in the super-deep ocean,” he says. “Imagining this happening is … pretty mind-boggling.”

A lot more work remains to be done to evaluate all of these new ideas, Stern says. “But a lot of things are now coming together.”

R. J. Stern et al. ROVing in the deep: tectonic and magmatic complexities of the Challenger Deep forearc segment, Southern Mariana convergent margin. Frontiers in Earth Science. 2026. doi: 10.3389/feart.2026.1929806

Carolyn Gramling is the earth & climate writer. She has bachelor’s degrees in geology and European history and a Ph.D. in marine geochemistry from MIT and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution.

#6242. Why a NASA spacecraft bound for Jupiter is on its way back to Earth

NASA’s Europa Clipper will fly past Earth on December 3 to gain speed and test its instruments before studying Jupiter’s icy moon Europa.

More than two years after leaving Earth, a spacecraft headed for Jupiter is about to pass within roughly 2,000 miles of home.

It has already traveled as far as Mars. Now it needs a close encounter with the planet it launched from to gain enough speed for the next leg of its journey.

NASA’s Europa Clipper is scheduled to make its closest approach west of Africa at 3:14 p.m. EST on December 3.

While Earth’s gravity bends its flight path, all nine science instruments will collect data.

For the scientists who will eventually study Jupiter’s icy moon Europa, the pass offers a chance to check how their instruments measure a world they already know.

Even after a spacecraft leaves Earth, it continues to travel around the Sun. Its speed and direction determine the shape of that orbit and how far from the Sun it can reach.

A close pass by a planet can change both, saving propellant that the spacecraft would otherwise need to make a similar maneuver with its engines.

As Clipper approaches Earth, gravity pulls the spacecraft toward the planet and curves its path. Earth is moving around the Sun the whole time.

The approach is timed so that this encounter transfers a tiny share of Earth’s orbital energy to Clipper, sending the spacecraft away at a higher speed around the Sun.

The geometry can also work in the opposite direction. When Clipper passed about 550 miles above Mars in March 2025, that encounter slowed the spacecraft and reshaped its orbit.

The new path brought it back toward Earth for the December flyby. By the time Clipper reaches Jupiter in April 2030, it will have covered about 1.8 billion miles.

On its way past Earth, Clipper will measure a magnetic field that scientists have spent decades mapping.

Engineers can compare those measurements with existing data to check the spacecraft’s magnetometer and refine its calibration.

At Europa, the same instrument will help scientists look for an ocean they can’t see.

The search depends on how saltwater responds to a changing magnetic field.

As Europa moves through Jupiter’s magnetic field, the field can drive electrical currents in a conductive ocean beneath the ice. Those currents would produce a magnetic signal of their own.

By measuring how that signal changes over repeated flybys, researchers hope to confirm the ocean is there and estimate its depth and salinity.

Clipper’s infrared camera will scan Earth every eight hours as the spacecraft approaches.

At Europa, it will map surface temperatures and look for areas that cool more slowly than their surroundings.

Those measurements can help scientists distinguish differences in the surface material and investigate whether any unusually warm spots point to activity below.

Comparing Clipper’s readings of Earth with observations from other spacecraft gives the team practice working with measurements taken from different vantage points.

Another gravity assist awaits Clipper at Jupiter. A close pass by Ganymede, the largest of Jupiter’s moons, will slow the spacecraft before it fires its engines to enter orbit around the planet.

From there, Clipper is set to make 49 flybys of Europa, some as low as 16 miles above the surface.

Each pass will take it over a different stretch of terrain, allowing scientists to piece together a picture of nearly the entire moon.

Europa’s surface is crossed by cracks and ridges. Some of the most revealing observations could come from looking at the same feature in several ways.

A camera can show where a ridge cuts across the ice, while temperature readings can reveal how quickly the surrounding ground cools.

Ice-penetrating radar can add a view beneath the surface, where echoes may reveal layers or pockets of liquid water.

Together with measurements of the moon’s composition, those observations could help scientists work out whether material moves between Europa’s surface and its ocean.

That exchange matters because liquid water is only one ingredient of a habitable environment. Life also needs a source of energy and chemicals it can use.

It will take years for Clipper to make those observations at Europa. On December 3, the team will start with a closer and more familiar target.

As the spacecraft heads outward again, it will carry a fresh set of measurements from Earth that will help scientists interpret what they eventually find beneath another world’s ice.

Speaking of iPhones, keep in mind that Apple generally doesn’t put its latest phones on sale, even on Black Friday. #6240. Big hope and lots of help for a tiny fish that lives in a desert cave

The endangered Devils Hole pupfish rebounded to 137 fish in October 2026, following captive-bred releases and feeding after earthquake damage.

Biologists counted 137 Devils Hole pupfish on Oct. 10, 2026, in the only place the species lives in the wild: a water-filled cavern in the Nevada desert.

The fall 2025 survey had found 69 fish, and the spring 2026 survey found 77, according to the National Park Service (NPS).

Devils Hole is a detached unit of Death Valley National Park. It opens onto an aquifer, and Ash Meadows is the discharge point for a groundwater system that reaches more than 100 miles (160 kilometers) to the northeast.

The cavern is more than 500 feet (152 meters) deep, and its bottom has never been mapped, according to the park’s Devils Hole page. The water stays at 92°F (33°C).

The fish forage and spawn on a shallow rock shelf near the surface, where they feed on algae and diatoms. That shelf, the population’s main feeding and breeding ground, covers about 215 square feet (20 square meters).

The fish are about 1 to 1.5 inches (2.5 to 3.8 centimeters) long. Males are iridescent blue, while females are olive-green.

The species has been isolated for 10,000 to 20,000 years, longer than any other pupfish in the Death Valley system. A presidential proclamation added Devils Hole to what was then Death Valley National Monument in 1952.

Scuba divers and surface counters from the NPS and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) survey the fish at the same time. Divers count in the cavern’s depths, while others watch the limestone shelf.

Biologists have used these methods nearly every spring and fall since 1972. Through the mid-1990s, counts averaged about 200 fish in spring and 425 in fall.

In the early 2000s, spring counts averaged about 90. The number dropped to 35 in spring 2013.

Pupfish numbers naturally rise and fall. The two agencies say continued monitoring, research and habitat management remain essential.

Two earthquakes, one in December and the other in February, set off waves in the cavern’s normally still water. The waves moved algae, organic material and fish eggs off the shelf.

A dive in March 2025 found only 20 or so fish. The official spring 2025 count recorded 38, down from 191 one year earlier.

“The present size at near-record lows deserves our serious attention, and the actions in the strategic plan, including supplemental feeding and population augmentation, provide the best opportunity for recovery,” Michael Schwemm, a senior fish biologist with the USFWS, said in April 2025.

“I’m proud of the work of this interagency team to monitor and protect the Devils Hole pupfish,” Mike Reynolds, superintendent of Death Valley National Park, said at the time.

An earthquake struck Panama, nearly 3,000 miles (4,800 kilometers) away, on Oct. 9, 2026, the day before the survey. Biologists first saw signs of stress in the fish, but a later visit found them in healthier condition.

Backup fish live at the Ash Meadows Fish Conservation Facility, built in 2013 with a Southern Nevada Public Land Management Act grant. Its refuge tank holds about 100,000 gallons (380,000 liters) and includes a replica of the Devils Hole habitat.

Staff collect eggs, aquatic invertebrates and algae from Devils Hole each month with NPS partners. They raise the young fish and add them to the refuge tank as young adults.

In spring 2025, biologists added captive-raised fish to the wild population for the first time. In all, 72 such fish were released into Devils Hole between March 2025 and February 2026.

Teams also fed the wild fish while the algae recovered, using data from the facility and from NPS monitoring.

“We were fortunate we had a strategic plan that allowed us to act cautiously but swiftly,” said Kevin Wilson, an aquatic ecologist and Devils Hole program manager at Death Valley National Park, in May 2026. That plan guided the step of “moving the refuge tank fish to Devils Hole to assist with recovery,” he said.

Schwemm said the 2022 plan “was instrumental in ensuring the wild population’s survival.”

The rebound followed those releases of captive-raised fish and the months of supplemental feeding in Devils Hole.

Still, the pupfish lives only 10 to 14 months on average. Biologists therefore believe most of the fish in the October count hatched and grew up in Devils Hole.

“It’s exciting to see Devils Hole pupfish numbers increase so significantly over the past year,” Reynolds said this fall.

“While challenges remain, we’re encouraged by this progress and committed to its long-term survival,” he added.

The species was listed as endangered in 1967. A 1976 court ruling in Cappaert v. United States recognized a water right for Devils Hole, and an injunction limited groundwater pumping to keep the shelf underwater.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service.

Live Science spoke with Nobel laureate Francis Halzen on how he got into physics "by accident" and built a neutrino detector that changed it forever.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When Francis Halzen first proposed burying a $271 million telescope deep beneath the South Pole, he expected to be laughed off stage. Four decades later, it won him a Nobel Prize.

Consisting of thousands of light sensors strung like rosary beads inside a cubic kilometer (0.2 cubic miles) of pristine ice, his detector, aptly named IceCube, is not an obvious way to study the universe. But Halzen, a theoretical physicist at the University of Madison-Wisconsin, isn't looking for something obvious.

His quarries are neutrinos, near-massless, chargeless, shapeshifters that are the most abundant material particles in existence. They form from nuclear processes and high-energy collisions, swarming out of our sun and whizzing from the outskirts of black holes. Yet though neutrinos stream through stars, planets, and us every second in their trillions, you still have a 75% chance of living your entire life without a single one striking an atom in your body.

On the rare occasions neutrinos do interact with atoms, they create charged particles that zip through water or ice faster than light does, casting a faint blue cone — the optical equivalent of a sonic boom.

Since 2011, IceCube has been retracing this blue light to study neutrinos produced by the most violent astrophysical events, probing energies far beyond those of Earth-based laboratories to find cracks in the laws of physics.

In the wake of his Nobel win, Live Science sat down with Halzen to discuss neutrinos, IceCube's journey from fanciful proposal to historic success, and the future of mapping the cosmos using the trails of ghosts. Here's what he had to say.

Ben Turner: What first got you into physics?

Francis Halzen: I got into physics kind of by accident. When I came out of high school, I didn't know what to do. I was interested in languages, I was interested in science. I'm a bad example of an inspirational career.

Francis Halzen is a Belgian-American particle physicist at the University of Wisconsin-Madinson who won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for his contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory. Halzen first proposed the telescope's prototype, called AMANDA, in 1988.

I did mathematics because in the Belgian system it was very much in the old French style — in fact, it was created by Napoleon — and hadn't changed when I was in high school. And so, if you were a good student, mathematics was the thing to do, right? So I did mathematics for two years, and then I did physics in parallel, and then switched to physics. When I switched, I got a professor who became my supervisor and he gave me the paper of George Zweig [who co-proposed quarks alongside Murray Gell-Mann] on quarks, which was a fundamental discovery.

George Zweig was actually an experimentalist, and he made these calculations using little figures. I recognized, as I had done mathematics, that this was group theory; and I said "I can do this better." I actually wrote several papers on the subject; and so suddenly I was a theoretical particle physicist. And that's what I still am. My heart never left particle physics.

BT: And then quarks eventually became neutrinos for you. Why neutrinos?

FH: I actually didn't study neutrinos until I really got involved in starting this experiment. Half of my career, which was passed by the time I started AMANDA [IceCube's prototype] and IceCube, I really had very little overlap with neutrino physics.

I became interested in neutrinos again [while] solving a theoretical problem. In fact, the idea of detecting neutrinos with ice originated with [Gurgen] Askaryan, an Armenian physicist, in 1963.

You cannot see neutrinos. They have no charge. They have basically no mass. So the way to detect neutrinos is when they interact with the nucleus. We are moving now in a sea of neutrinos, but neutrinos don't interact with atoms, so we don't know it. But if they accidentally hit the nucleus of an atom, then they make a nuclear reaction, and that emits charged particles. It's like a spark, and you can detect a spark with antennas.

So Askaryan's idea was to put radio antennas in ice. We are doing exactly that. But instead of looking at the radio emission, we look at the light that's emitted, which is just blue light. We use that blue light to reconstruct the neutrino and all its properties, including its direction — [that's] why it is a telescope, right?

Building on Askaryan's idea, The Askaryan Radio Array (ARA) complements IceCube by searching for high-energy neutrinos with radio antennas buried 200 meters (670 feet) below Antarctica's ice.

I was worrying about that experiment because they had not been able to calculate the power of the spark, so they didn't know if this worked or not. Then someone told me at some point that the Russians — I guess it was still the Soviet Union — are actually doing this at a station in Antarctica by pointing [radio] dishes into the ice. I said: "This is crazy."

But I had ice all over my brain, right? When I saw in the late 80s how difficult it was to do these experiments in deep ocean water it was normal to have the idea to do it in ice. And, to our credit, we understood that it actually may be simpler.

BT: Why is being able to calculate the power of the spark so important?

FH: [It's about] how much light is made, and how far it travels through your detector. If you don't make enough light, and it's immediately absorbed, then you have no experiment.

The reason we are talking to each other [today] is because we had this incredible luck that blue light travels 100 meters [328 feet] and more through this ancient ice without being absorbed. So it's relatively easy to instrument an ice block of a kilometer cubed with light sensors.

BT: When you first proposed melting 61 two-kilometre [1.2-mile] holes in the coldest place on Earth, you said you expected to be laughed off stage. Then when you weren't, you said you continued to worry about it. What were you worrying about?

FH: Well, the worry was that I was totally out of my league. I didn't understand glaciology, I am not an experimentalist, so I didn't really grasp the technological challenges of doing this. The experiments in water were not doing very well: There was the leading experiment off the coast of Hawaii [the Deep Underwater Muon And Neutrino Detector, or DUMAND, project] and it happened that the man leading this experiment, John Learned, was a good friend of mine, and I eventually contacted him.

And the glaciology, of course. Nobody knew what the optical properties were of ice at a depth of one kilometer [0.6 miles] or more under the South Pole. There were [ice] cores that had been taken, but cores are small — the size of a teacup — so you cannot tell how far the light travels [through the ice]. So people thought it was a cute idea that would never work.

If I had known more about glaciology, about hot water drilling, and about the technical challenges, I would never have started this experiment. It's the advantage of being ignorant. It's why young people make great discoveries, and when you're 82 years old you don't make this progress — you know too much.

An artist's illustration showing what the interior of IceCube would look like without the ice.

BT: You speak about AMANDA and IceCube with a lot of ambivalence. You said you "got dragged into it by accident" and "tried to get out of it many times."

FH: Oh yes, absolutely. You know, theorists write two types of papers: [the first are] papers where they think they contribute to the progress of science — they usually don't. But the other type of paper is just to show you're smart. And this was definitely in the second category. And then two people from Berkeley [Doug Lowder and Andrew Westphal] actually started the experiment.

BT: Well, you won a Nobel Prize for it. If you wanted to look smart, you succeeded.

FH: Yeah, without a lot of luck, I wouldn't be sitting here.

They're this almost non-existent piece of reality.

BT: But surely it wasn't just showing off? Despite all of the uncertainties and worries, there must have been something about neutrinos — these barely detectable, misbehaving particles — that's so important it made you stick around. What's the draw to learn about them?

FH: Neutrinos are something really special, right? When you look at the Standard Model of matter [which describes all the known particles and forces], it has quarks, leptons, and neutrinos.

But neutrinos are special in the sense that they're supposed to have no mass. They're just like photons: they travel at the speed of light, so you can do astronomy with them. But then they have the advantage that they go through planets; they go through the Earth; they reach you from the beginning of time; they reach you from the edge of the universe. They're this almost non-existent piece of reality.

So they always had a special fascination. We knew they existed since 1930; because without neutrinos you cannot change a proton into a neutron. They were ghosts — that's where the name "ghost particle" comes from. They were part of physics, and particle physics, and nuclear physics, but they had never been seen.

It's only in 1956 that [Frederick] Reines and [Clyde] Cowen finally discovered the neutrino by putting a detector close to a nuclear reactor, where there are lots of them. If they don't interact, then you compensate by going to a place where there are lots of them, and a nuclear reactor was an opportunity.

It's a fascinating particle. Of course now it fascinates us because they do have mass, which is not allowed by the structure of the Standard Model, and so they carry some information on new physics — the new physics we are looking for with the Large Hadron Collider in Geneva. They are the particles that have carried the message of that new physics most directly, and that's our domain.

We should have all the advantages. Sadly, they just behave like the Standard Model in everything we have done over the first 15 years of this experiment.

Construction workers inside one of the two colossal caverns created for the particle detector modules of Fermilab's Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE). By probing the properties of neutrinos, physicists are hoping to assess key theories, including neutrinos' hypothesized role in tipping the universe into containing more matter than antimatter.

BT: Famously, in 1993 to '94, microscopic air bubbles trapped in Antarctica's ice scattered neutrinos' blue light like frosted glass, nearly killing the project. You saved it by drilling to where the ice sheet's weight crushed those bubbles out of existence, up to 2.5 kilometers [1.6 miles] beneath the surface and one kilometer deeper than you originally planned. How hard was that?

FH: Well, the drilling almost killed the project twice.

It's actually an interesting story, because we now detect a neutrino every minute as we are speaking, but they are produced in the atmosphere. They [atmospheric neutrinos] are our background — interesting background, but a background.

As energetic particles called cosmic rays strike Earth's upper atmosphere, they create showers of smaller particles, including neutrinos, that can be detected on the surface. IceCube's scientists filter out lower-energy atmospheric neutrinos (alongside those produced by the sun) to find only those made in astrophysical cataclysms.

After we had solved all these problems and could detect neutrinos, the only threshold to cross was to produce a drill that could build IceCube. That involves melting ice over two and a half kilometers over an area the size of a basketball. The technique existed in glaciers, but [produced] a shallow hole about the size of a bottle of wine.

So we went to companies specialized in building hoses, and we needed a hose that was 2.5 kilometers long. The first company we went to told us: "Look, you hang a hose the size of a tea cup over two and a half kilometers of hot water and what do you think will happen?" It will collapse. Even the theorists could understand that it would collapse.

And that was the end of the project. For weeks I thought it was finished. I told one of our engineers, a brilliant guy who contributed much more than what I'm going to tell you, and he didn't give up. He found a company in Padua, Italy, near Venice and they said: "We can build anything." And they did.

Then, when we started drilling, it was still a problem. We drilled one hole over a whole [South Pole] season. We had brilliant engineers working on this totally new piece of equipment — you have no idea how complex this is — and they learned from the mistakes of the first year and the second year it worked. They deployed 86 strings without ever failing, which is amazing actually. It's like when you launch 86 satellites, you're probably going to fail some. That's what we thought. But they never did.

A view down along one of IceCube's 86 detector strings, dangling in holes drilled up to 2.5 kilometers into the ice.

BT: The detector went online in 2011, then that year and the next came "Bert" and "Ernie" — the first ever detections of astrophysical neutrinos from beyond our solar system. After all that effort, all those near misses, and every doubt you ever had, what did it feel like when they arrived?

FH: We were not sure we believed it. It was clear then that this was a major discovery — if it was true. It took us six months or more to have the courage to write the paper.

I remember seeing the first events on my screen in October of 2012, and they looked like they couldn't have come from the atmosphere — such high energy! We discovered the first two serendipitously in the first two years of data. Then, after we went to look for more knowing what these events look like, we had 28. So we had the courage to publish.

But then, three weeks later, we were declared the physics breakthrough of the year. I must say I was not happy about that. I had to give a press conference, and I was all the time thinking: "If this is not true, how am I going to walk this back?"

It took me quite a while to convince myself that this wasn't just something that looked like cosmic neutrinos. But this is such an unusual corner of science, you don't know whether you are fooled by some other phenomena you haven't thought of.

FH: Well now we are seeing sources of neutrinos. You see 100 neutrinos come from an active galaxy, and you point [a different telescope] back at it with 0.04 degree resolution. There's no doubt now. But being convinced was a continuous process; at least in my case. My colleagues always refer to me as a total optimist, but it took me some time. I was not my usual self on this.

But now there's no doubt. The statistics of observing cosmic neutrinos is totally impossible [to deny] with the precision we have now. But we're talking about 14 years of data. It's really incredible how quickly we've progressed.

A crane deploys the Baikal-GVD neutrino telescope from the ice cover of Lake Baikal, Siberia.

And you realize that, officially, none of the things we see have been confirmed by someone else. There are two experiments, [Baikal-G in Lake Baikal and [KM3NeT] in the Mediterranean Sea, but they're under construction. And they both have produced some kind of evidence, but a real confirmation of seeing the same thing we see has still not happened. So the Nobel Prize [Committee] had more courage than me.

I had forgotten that it was Nobel season.

BT: You were in a hotel room in Italy when the call came from Stockholm. What went through your mind in the first quiet moments after hanging up?

FH: Well, after hanging up, I was sent a Zoom link, and they asked me questions, which I answered. But I didn't know that I was actually giving a press conference. I still haven't looked back at that press conference.

But that's how crazy it was, because I had forgotten that it was Nobel season. The call came by total surprise. Well, it wasn't a total surprise because there's a game of predicting the Nobel Prizes. And I had been there [in the running to win] for several years.

So I cannot say that I was unaware of this. But this was a difficult season for me, right? People literally would send me condolence messages every year for not winning. And they meant it — they're my friends — but it makes you feel strange. You feel you've disappointed your collaborators.

So that's the first thing I thought: "Okay, the problem is solved now. Everybody can get credit for this experiment." And deservedly. Because IceCube was becoming mostly me, and data and science. The fact of its history and the contributions people made was being forgotten very fast. The great thing about this Nobel Prize is that it's for a difficult problem that was solved by so many brilliant people over almost four decades.

BT: Aside from winning the Nobel, what's been the highlight of working on IceCube?

FH: The highlight for me was to show that the technique works. Seeing these neutrinos go through the Earth, and then through the detector, was incredibly exciting because there was no doubt you were looking at a stream of particles going through your detector initiated by neutrinos that came through the Earth. There was no doubt. What you see is what you get.

We had this attitude that if you build something this big you're going to do interesting science. This is so different from anything that has been built before. I don't want to insult astronomers, but our joke was: "We are all particle physicists, guys. God forbid we have to do astronomy." But that's what we are doing.

I must say, it's very, very exciting to learn astronomy when you're 82 years old.

BT: IceCube–Gen2 is targeted to come online by 2033 and will be eight times larger than the original detector. What do you want for its future?

FH: Whenever I give a talk, I have a list of conclusions, and my first is always that neutrino astronomy exists, and that's our contribution. Doing neutrino astronomy will require more instruments, bigger instruments. In astronomy there's not just one telescope, right? To do real astronomy we'll need more instruments covering the sky completely, and we'll need more neutrinos with better angular resolution.

The nice thing is that will happen: There are ambitious projects in China now, and [the upgrade of] our own project too. How can you pass it up? Because now the technology is much better: we understand the ice perfectly; we can design this detector, optimize it, and gain an order of magnitude [improvement] for the same cost as the original.

China's Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory (JUNO) detector while it was under construction in 2024. The detector, which is designed to probe neutrinos from space and from Earth, came online in August 2026.

BT: You famously don't like to make predictions, even one year ahead, about what we might learn about neutrinos. So I'm going to try to be sly with this final question: What do you hope the future has in store for neutrino astronomy?

FH: I hope for a galactic supernova [within the Milky Way]. I don't know if you know the history, but in 1987 there was a supernova in a [nearby] satellite galaxy, but it [meant physicists] detected 20 neutrinos. And what we learned from these neutrinos is incredible — literally thousands of papers have been written about those 20 neutrinos, and they're all interesting.

Neutrinos are supposed to have no mass and be just like photons. The best limit we could set on the [tiny and still unexplained] mass of the neutrino came from that supernova. So we made very fundamental measurements that we hadn't been able to make with [laboratory] neutrino beams. And then the whole story that a star really collapses into a neutron star. All that suddenly became reality. I was not, and am still not, an astronomer, but from the point of view of stellar physics this was a major event.

Now, instead of three experiments, we have multiple neutrino detectors of all kinds. Some will detect thousands of neutrinos; we'll detect a million neutrinos. We can't actually reconstruct them, but we can make a very detailed movie telling you everything that went on in a supernova while the star collapsed and then exploded. The science we will do from a few seconds of data will be incredible.

I can tell you it hasn't happened since the mid-1990s because we have been looking for it continuously with AMANDA and Ice-Cube. There are supposed to be like two per century. We are due.

Editor's note: This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Ben Turner is the features editor at Live Science. He covers physics and astronomy, among other topics such as tech and climate change. He graduated from University College London with a degree in particle physics before training as a journalist. When he's not writing, Ben enjoys reading literature, playing the guitar and losing at chess.

#6238. The earliest corporate psychopath on record may have been been this traitor from the 1600s

A management researcher scored a 1629 mutiny leader against a modern corporate psychopath checklist, and he matched all ten traits.

For about 30 years, researchers have studied corporate psychopaths. They are the charming, ruthless bosses who rule by fear and blame everyone else. Most of the examples that come to mind are usually living or recent executives.

Now the earliest one on record may be a merchant who ran a survivors’ camp after a 1629 wreck. Scored against a ten-item checklist built for today’s boardrooms, Jeronimus Cornelisz of the Dutch East India Company matches every item.

Clive Boddy, an associate professor of management at Anglia Ruskin University in England, wrote the paper alone. Boddy has spent years studying corporate psychopathy.

This paper is a historical case study rather than an experiment. It leans mainly on the historian Mike Dash’s 2003 book about the wreck.

Other sources are the expedition commander’s journal, a pastor’s letters, trial records, and skeletons dug up on the island.

“What makes this case remarkable is that when we analyzed Cornelisz using a modern management psychopathy framework, he displayed every major characteristic associated with corporate psychopaths,” Boddy said.

The Batavia was the company’s new flagship, bound for the port the Dutch had renamed Batavia, now Jakarta.

On the morning of June 4, 1629, it struck a reef in the Houtman Abrolhos islands. The reef lies 80 miles (130 kilometers) off Western Australia, and most of the people aboard managed to reach a small coral island.

Somewhere between 180 and 250 people made it ashore, and 30 of them were women and children. The island had no fresh water of its own.

The commander, Francisco Pelsaert, the ship’s captain, and 46 others then left in an overloaded longboat to fetch help from Jakarta, 900 miles (1,450 kilometers) away.

That left Cornelisz, a junior merchant and the most senior company man still on the island, in charge of everyone else.

Cornelisz had been plotting a mutiny before the ship went down. Once in command, Boddy wrote, he replaced the lawful council with his fellow plotters and had them swear personal oaths of loyalty.

He moved the money chests, water, and food into his own tent, and the plan was to seize whatever rescue ship arrived and turn pirate.

He also sent groups of survivors to two other islands, supposedly to look for water, and left them there. Then he told his followers that the island’s population had to shrink if supplies were to last.

Between 96 and 115 men, women, and children were murdered over the following weeks, and some of the women were subjected to sexual violence.

Cornelisz ordered the killings and, with one exception, left others to carry them out. A pastor who survived wrote that the remaining people lived in constant fear of being next.

In Boddy’s reading, that climate of fear is the same tool corporate psychopaths use to keep a workforce in line.

The soldiers Cornelisz had dumped on the farthest island did not die. Their island had two freshwater wells, seabird colonies, fish, wallabies, and seals.

Under a soldier named Wiebbe Hayes, the group of 46 men and a boy fed itself and took in people who escaped the killings.

When word of the murders reached them, Hayes had his men forge pikes from wreckage, pile up coral to throw, and build a small stone fort on a hill.

They turned back two raids, captured Cornelisz during a third attempt, and were holding off a fourth, this time against muskets, when the rescue ship appeared. Hayes’s men reached it first and warned the crew.

Cornelisz and his ringleaders were tried on the spot, confessed, and were hanged. Hayes was promoted.

Boddy calls the two islands a natural experiment in leadership: same wreck, same weather, and one group built cooperation and found food while the other descended into murder.

The checklist is a ten-item measure of what researchers call primary psychopathy, written for management research rather than for prisons.

Boddy’s rule for judging someone from history is that they must clearly show at least eight of the ten. The same test has been applied to the financier Bernard Madoff, the media owner Robert Maxwell, and the Nazi leader Hermann Goering.

Cornelisz scores on all ten in the paper’s table of characteristics shown by corporate psychopaths. The items include superficial charm, habitual lying, total self-regard, no remorse, and shallow emotion.

They end with a calm, rational manner while ordering murders, and no insight into his own behavior. Dash had already called Cornelisz a psychopath on an informal reading of the criminal criteria.

Boddy’s paper is the first to run him through a management measure item by item. The record it draws on includes the wreck itself, found by divers in 1963 and partly reconstructed by the Western Australian Museum.

Boddy also visited the Museum of Geraldton, which holds finds from the wreck, as background.

Everything in the assessment comes from documents and from one historian’s account of them. There is no way to interview, test, or observe the man himself, and the paper reports no new data and has no limitations section of its own.

Prevalence is the other open number. About 1 percent of adults are usually counted as categorically psychopathic, and a newer pooled analysis that used non-criminal measures found 4.5 percent. Either way, the share is small in the general population.

Among senior corporate leaders, one estimate comes to about 4 percent, with some industries drawing more of the money-hungry personality than others. How many of them run companies today isn’t something a shipwreck from 1629 can say.

Boddy’s next candidate is another company man, Governor General Jan Coen, who ordered massacres while building the Dutch spice monopoly.

The paper closes by asking personnel departments to weigh character and values when they pick senior leaders. The pattern it describes, Boddy wrote, has apparently been in place since the first shareholder-owned company existed.

The full study was published in the journal Asian Journal of Business Ethics.

#6237. ‘Mitt & Ted’ recounts how a political odd couple changed U.S. health care

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The Big Dig podcast host Ian Coss explores how Mitt Romney and Ted Kennedy worked together to reform American health care laws

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In 1973, U.S. Senator Ted Kennedy often visited the cancer ward at Boston Children’s Hospital, where his eldest son was battling osteosarcoma. Kennedy witnessed other parents on the ward make impossible decisions regarding their child’s care when insurance didn’t cover it. Their stories lit a fire within the senator that burned bright for the rest of his life.

Kennedy spent decades fighting for health care reform, representing his home state of Massachusetts. He even teamed up with a former political rival from across the aisle: Mitt Romney. The story of this unexpected alliance is recounted in Mitt & Ted, the newest season of the GBH News podcast The Big Dig. Over eight episodes, journalist and host Ian Coss explores how their work laid the foundation for the Affordable Care Act, one of the most significant and divisive health care reforms in U.S. history.

We first meet Romney as a young upstart Republican challenger vying to flip Kennedy’s Senate seat in 1994. The race seemed close until a legendary debate. Romney had Kennedy on the defensive until the sitting senator pivoted to the issue near and dear to his heart: health care.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“Kennedy is the elder statesman, in command of the issue,” Coss says. “Romney is like an eager student trying to pass the test.” Using his deep knowledge, Kennedy buries the less experienced Romney. In the election, Kennedy then beat Romney by a landslide, even when many Democrats were ousted by Republican challengers that same year. But the loss may have motivated Romney to keep going.

Several years later, Romney unexpectedly became a champion of health care reform as the newly elected governor of Massachusetts. The state’s health care system was facing the potential loss of about a billion dollars in federal funding, threatening hospitals that served vulnerable populations. Romney’s administration created Romneycare, which was supported by three features: individual and employer mandates, affordable options for low-income people, and a health care exchange where people could compare plans from different providers.

With Senator Kennedy’s help, the groundbreaking law passed in 2006 and expanded health insurance coverage to 98 percent of Massachusetts’ population.

Romneycare gained national attention and kicked off years-long efforts to replicate it on the federal level. Finally, in 2010, President Obama signed the Affordable Care Act, or ACA. Modeled on Romneycare, the law (colloquially called Obamacare) adapted the reforms made in Massachusetts for all 50 states, a challenge since many states had larger shares of uninsured people than Massachusetts had even before Romneycare.

The Democrats in Congress also sought to include a government insurance plan in the reform, similar to Medicaid but available to more people. Republicans were wary of the ACA generally, but a government-provided insurance option was a line they wouldn’t cross. The ACA eventually passed without the public option, but by then the political winds had shifted. If there ever was a chance to secure bipartisan support for the law, it was gone by the time Democrats were willing to compromise on the public option. And as soon as the ACA became law, Republicans started fighting it.

The podcast traces an impressive number of political twists and turns on this health care reform journey. Though I got turned around a few times, I never fully lost the plot thanks to Coss’ well-placed reminders and takeaways.

Beyond the story of Romney and Kennedy, the podcast gives voice to many more people who made the ACA a reality: government workers who went from foes to allies who enlisted unlikely help from the conservative Heritage Foundation; longtime friends in the Massachusetts state legislature who were driven apart by the reform; a father who struggled to afford health care and how he advocated for reform with his church. I teared up more than once listening to the human stories behind these policy changes.

Overall, Mitt & Ted gave me new appreciation for why passing a reform is so difficult, despite how life-changing and life-saving access to health care can be. The series points to moments when stars aligned to make reform possible and suggests that more of those opportunities lie ahead.

“The work of American health care remains very much unfinished,” Coss says. “When the perfect alignment of frustration and opportunity arrives again, that might be what determines whether our leaders actually work together.”

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

Lily Burton was the Spring 2026 science writing intern at Science News. She holds a bachelor’s degree in Molecular and Cell Biology and Anthropology from UC Berkeley. She also has a Ph.D. in Biochemistry and Molecular Biophysics from the University of Chicago where she researched circadian rhythms in photosynthetic bacteria and the role they play in metabolism. She was a 2024 AAAS Mass Media Fellow where she reported on local science at WUNC – North Carolina Public Radio.
